chapters.title: Centre of Mass, Linear Momentum, Collision
chapters.summary: This chapter introduces the concept of centre of mass for collections of particles and extended bodies, showing how it simplifies the analysis of complex motion. It develops the principle of conservation of linear momentum and applies these ideas to analyse various types of collisions.

events.text: The centre of mass moves like a single thrown particle, however the rest spins
COM = mass-weighted average position
dm = a tiny piece of the rod
X = (1/M) integral of x dm
Q: Find the centre of mass of a uniform rod of mass M and length L.
dm = (M/L) dx, element at (x, 0, 0)
X = (1/M) ∫ x dm = (1/M) ∫₀ᴸ x (M/L) dx
Centre of mass at (L/2, 0, 0) — the middle of the rod
Q: Find the centre of mass of a uniform semicircular wire, mass M, radius R.
element length = R d theta, theta from 0 to pi
element at (R cos theta, R sin theta)
X = (1/M) ∫₀^π (R cos theta)(M/pi) d theta = 0
Y = (1/M) ∫₀^π (R sin theta)(M/pi) d theta = 2R/pi
Centre of mass at (0, 2R/pi)
Q: Find centre of mass of a uniform semicircular plate, mass M, radius R
Element = semicircular ring between r and r + dr
Area of plate = pi R squared over 2, so mass per area = M / (pi R squared / 2)
y of each wire = 2r/pi; integrate r from 0 to R
Y = 4R / (3 pi),  X = 0 by symmetry
centre of mass can sit in empty space
Internal forces come in equal, opposite pairs
m one times a one equals plus F, m two times a two equals minus F
No external force, then the centre of mass never accelerates
Q: Masses m and 2m, distance d apart on a frictionless table, attract and collide. Where do they collide?
External force on system = 0, so a of centre of mass = 0
Both start at rest, so velocity of centre of mass = 0, centre of mass stays fixed
At collision both particles coincide with centre of mass, so collision occurs at the centre of mass
Collision occurs at the centre of mass, 2d/3 from the mass m, toward the mass 2m
diver's centre of mass = clean parabola
Total momentum = total mass times velocity of centre of mass
No external force means total momentum is constant
Q: A nucleus at rest emits an alpha particle (mass m, speed v); find the recoil speed V of the residual nucleus (mass M).
System = whole nucleus; only internal forces, no external force ⇒ momentum conserved
p_before = 0
V = - (m/M) v
Boy's forward momentum is cancelled by the board's backward momentum
Total momentum before = total momentum after = 0
Q: Shuttle at 4000 km/h ejects 1/6 of its mass backward at 100 km/h relative to shuttle. Find final shuttle speed V.
module velocity (rel. earth) = -100 + 4000 = 3900 km/h
V = 4020 km/h
Q: Boy 25 kg on board 10 kg on frictionless ice; boy jumps at 5 m/s. Find board recoil and separation rate.
System = board + boy; no horizontal external force, so horizontal momentum is conserved.
Board recoil v = 12.5 m/s; separation rate = 5 + 12.5 = 17.5 m/s
Q: Man (mass m) on platform (mass M) on smooth ice; man moves at speed v relative to platform. Find platform recoil V relative to ice.
V + w = v, so w = v − V
0 = MV − mw
MV = m(v − V) → V(M + m) = mv
V = mv / (M + m)
Q: Mass m at velocity v hits mass 2m at rest; first stops, 2m splits into two equal pieces m each; one piece moves along Y at v1. Find the other piece's velocity.
Before: p = m v along X-axis
After: first ball 0; piece 1 = m v1 along Y; piece 2 = m v2 at angle theta
X-axis: m v2 cos(theta) = m v
Y-axis: m v2 sin(theta) = m v1
Square and add: v2^2 = v^2 + v1^2
Divide: tan(theta) = v1 / v
v2 = sqrt(v^2 + v1^2), at angle theta with tan(theta) = v1/v
Q: Bullet (0.05 kg) embeds in bob (0.45 kg); bob rises 1.8 m. Find bullet speed. g = 10 m/s^2
v = 60 m/s
Q: Spring (constant k) compressed by x between blocks m and M on a smooth surface, released from rest. Find final speeds.
M V − m v = 0  ⟹  V = (m/M) v
½ m v² + ½ M V² = ½ k x²
Substitute V = (m/M)v, then solve for v
Q: Blocks m and M joined by spring k on smooth plane; constant force F pulls M from rest. Find max extension.
Take system = both blocks + spring; centre of mass acceleration a = F / (m + M)
Effective force on each block = mF / (m + M)
Maximum extension = 2mF / (k(m + M))
Q: Ball A moves right at v, ball B at rest, fixed wall at right, all collisions elastic. Show final speeds unchanged.
Final speeds unchanged: both balls move at speed v, same as initial.
Q: mass m at velocity v hits mass 2m at rest head-on, restitution = 1/2; find final velocities
m v = m u1 + 2m u2
v = u1 + 2u2, with u2 = u1 + v/2
Q: 1.2 kg block at 20 cm/s hits identical block at rest, e = 3/5. Find KE lost.
v1 = 4 cm/s,  v2 = 16 cm/s
Loss of KE = 7.7 × 10⁻³ J
Q: Ball of mass m hits floor at speed v, angle theta with normal, restitution e. Find reflected speed and angle.
v' sin(theta') = v sin(theta)
v' cos(theta') = e v cos(theta)
v' = v * sqrt(sin^2(theta) + e^2 cos^2(theta))
v' = v*sqrt(sin^2(theta) + e^2 cos^2(theta)),  tan(theta') = tan(theta)/e
Q: Block (m) and pan (m) over a smooth light pulley, at rest. Particle (m) hits the pan at speed v and sticks. Find the speed V just after collision.
Particle: ∫N dt = mv − mV
Pan: ∫(N − T) dt = mV
Block: ∫T dt = mV
Add pan + block: ∫N dt = 2mV
Compare: mv − mV = 2mV → mv = 3mV
V = v/3
step off canoe, boat recoils
Throw gas backward, get shoved forward
Lighter rocket, bigger acceleration
No air needed — pushes its own exhaust
rear block m1 fast, front block m2 slow
Spring force on each block is equal and opposite, so total momentum is conserved
At maximum compression both blocks share one common velocity
Elastic means no kinetic energy lost
Divide the energy equation by the momentum equation
v one minus v two equals v two prime minus v one prime
Q: Heavy body A (mass much greater than B) hits light body B from behind. Find final velocities.
v1 prime is approximately v1
v2 prime is approximately two v1 minus v2
Set v2 = 0, then v2 prime = two v1
v1 prime is approximately v1, and v2 prime is approximately two v1 (when v2 = 0)
Q: Light body A (mass m1) hits heavy body B (mass m2, with m2 much greater than m1) from behind. Find the final velocities.
v1' is approximately equal to negative v1 plus two times v2
v2' is approximately equal to v2
If v2 = 0, then v1' = negative v1 (A bounces back with the same speed); v2' is approximately v2
Q: Equal masses, elastic collision in 1D — find final velocities
Set m of A = m of B in the elastic collision equations
v1' = v2 and v2' = v1 — equal masses exchange their velocities
equal masses swap velocities
one in, one out — momentum AND energy must both balance
Objects stick, move as one
Before equals after: m1 v1 plus m2 v2 equals (m1 plus m2) V
V equals total momentum over total mass
KE lost to heat, sound, deformation
Momentum conserved, KE lost
Real collisions: part bouncy, part squishy
e = velocity of separation / velocity of approach
Q: Mass m at speed v hits mass 2m at rest; the first block stops. Find e.
Conservation of momentum: m times v = two m times v prime
v prime = v over two
velocity of separation = v over two;  velocity of approach = v
e = (v over two) divided by v = one half
Momentum is conserved along X and along Y, separately

Impulse = area under the force-time curve = change in momentum
No outside sideways force means total momentum is conserved

events.text: Centre of mass keeps moving exactly as before
Internal pushes cancel in pairs

chapters.narration_text:
<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics:centre_of_mass_linear_momentum_collision:9_1>>
<<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:centre_of_mass_linear_momentum_collision:9_1:spinning_ball_paths>> Throw a spinning cricket ball into the air, and pick <<FOCUS:surface-dot>> one tiny freckle on its surface. <<UNFOCUS>> That speck traces a path so tangled you could never write it down. Watch it <<TRACE:surface-tangled-path>> loop and coil through space as the ball spins and rises. <<UNFOCUS>> It is a genuine mess. So here is the honest question: if every point on a spinning, tumbling object moves in such a complicated way, is there any part of it that moves simply? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<SECTION:The special point|id=sec-1>> There is. One single point inside the ball ignores all the spinning and <<TRACE:centre-parabola>> traces a clean, smooth parabola, exactly like a stone thrown through the air. <<PAUSE:short>> Watch <<FOCUS:centre-dot>> this central dot glide along its simple arc while <<FOCUS:surface-dot>> the surface freckle thrashes around it. <<UNFOCUS>> The spinner's fingers cannot disturb this point at all. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:The centre of mass moves like a single thrown particle, however the rest spins|id=key-1>> This special point is <<FOCUS:centre-dot>> called the centre of mass, and its motion is just like the motion of a single particle thrown into the air. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> That is why it matters so much. Instead of tracking every messy point of a complicated body, we track this one point and the whole object's motion becomes simple. <<PAUSE:short>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:centre_of_mass_linear_momentum_collision:9_1:two_mass_balance>> <<SECTION:Where does it sit?|id=sec-2>> But where exactly is this point? Let us strip away the ball and use the simplest case: <<FOCUS:connecting-rod>> two masses joined by a light rod. Here is a <<FOCUS:mass-heavy>> heavy mass on the left and <<FOCUS:mass-light>> a light mass on the right. <<UNFOCUS>> If you tried to balance this rod on your finger, where would the balance point be? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> Not in the middle. It sits <<FOCUS:com-marker+mass-heavy>> closer to the heavier mass, because that side carries more of the total. So the centre of mass is just <<FOCUS:com-marker+position-axis>> a weighted average of position: each particle's location, weighted by how much mass it carries, divided by the total mass. <<UNFOCUS>> For two masses, take each mass times its position, add them, and divide by the total mass. <<WRITE_EQUATION:x_{cm} = \dfrac{m_1 x_1 + m_2 x_2}{m_1 + m_2}|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<WRITE_TEXT:COM = mass-weighted average position|id=text-1>> Heavier things pull the average toward themselves, which is exactly why the <<FOCUS:com-marker+mass-heavy>> balance point hugs the big mass. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> For any number of particles, add up every mass times its position and divide by the total mass. <<WRITE_EQUATION:x_{cm} = \dfrac{\sum m_i x_i}{\sum m_i}|id=eq-2|boxed>> And that single point, this weighted average, is the very thing that <<FOCUS:com-marker>> glides along the clean parabola while the whole object dances around it.

<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics:centre_of_mass_linear_momentum_collision:9_2>>
<<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:centre_of_mass_linear_momentum_collision:9_2:rod_slice>> You know how to balance two weights on a seesaw, but where exactly does a smooth, solid rod balance, when there are no separate weights at all? <<PAUSE:long>> Up to now we found the centre of mass by adding up separate particles, one mass here, another mass there. But <<FOCUS:rod-body>> this rod isn't chunks, it's matter spread out smoothly, with no gaps to point at. <<UNFOCUS>> So here is the whole idea: if we can't point at separate pieces, we'll make our own. <<PAUSE:short>> <<SECTION:Slicing the rod|id=sec-slice>> Watch <<FOCUS:slice-element>> this thin slice. We cut out one tiny piece of the rod between position x and a tiny bit further along, and we call its tiny mass dm. <<PAUSE:short>> <<ANIMATE_PARAM:x_pos|to=0.95|from=0.05|duration=2200>> <<WRITE_TEXT:dm = a tiny piece of the rod|id=text-dm>> Now I'll slide that slice along the rod, and as it sweeps from the left end all the way to the right end, those tiny pieces cover the entire body. Each slice sits at <<FOCUS:slice-position>> its own distance x from the origin, and that distance is exactly what we measure here. <<UNFOCUS>> Because the rod is uniform, every centimetre carries the same mass, so the mass of a slice is the mass per unit length times the slice's tiny width. <<WRITE_EQUATION:dm = \frac{M}{L}\,dx|id=eq-1|boxed>> So here's the honest question: if every slice has its own little mass dm at its own position x, how do we possibly combine all of them into one balance point? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> We add them up. Each slice contributes its position x times its mass dm, and we sum that over every slice in the body. That continuous summing-up is exactly what integration means. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:X = (1/M) integral of x dm|id=key-com>> Then we divide by the total mass M, and out pops the single x-coordinate of the centre of mass. <<PAUSE:short>> The x-coordinate of the centre of mass is the sum of each slice's position times its mass, divided by the total mass. <<WRITE_EQUATION:X = \frac{1}{M}\int x\,dm|id=eq-2|boxed>> The recipe never changes: pick a clever slice, find its mass dm, find where it sits, then integrate over the whole body. Here's an example from the chapter: finding the centre of mass of a uniform straight rod. Let M and L be the mass and the length of the rod respectively. We take the <<FOCUS:origin-mark>> left end of the rod as the origin, with the X-axis running along the rod. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Find the centre of mass of a uniform rod of mass M and length L.|id=ex-q-1>> We start by <<FOCUS:slice-element>> slicing the rod into a thin element between the positions x and x plus dx. <<UNFOCUS>> Since the rod is uniform, the mass per unit length is M divided by L, so the mass of this little element is dm equals M over L times dx. The <<FOCUS:slice-position>> coordinates of the element are x, zero, zero. <<WRITE_STEP:dm = (M/L) dx, element at (x, 0, 0)|id=ex-step-1-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> Now the x-coordinate of the centre of mass is one over M times the integral of x dm. Substituting dm equals M over L times dx, and letting x vary from zero to L, this becomes one over M times the integral from zero to L of x times M over L dx. <<WRITE_STEP:X = (1/M) ∫ x dm = (1/M) ∫₀ᴸ x (M/L) dx|id=ex-step-1-2>> The M's cancel, leaving one over L times x squared over two, evaluated from zero to L. Plugging in the limits gives one over L times L squared over two, which simplifies to L over two. <<WRITE_STEP:X = (1/L)[x²/2]₀ᴸ = L/2|id=ex-step-1-3>> By symmetry the y-coordinate is zero and the z-coordinate is zero as well. So the answer is that the centre of mass sits at L over two, zero, zero, <<FOCUS:com-point>> exactly the middle point of the rod. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Centre of mass at (L/2, 0, 0) — the middle of the rod|id=ex-ans-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> Here's an example from the chapter. We have a uniform semicircular wire of mass M and radius R. We take its centre as the origin, with the line joining the ends along the X-axis, and the Y-axis in the plane of the wire. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Find the centre of mass of a uniform semicircular wire, mass M, radius R.|id=ex-q-1>> We start by picking an element. Take a radius making an angle theta with the X-axis, and rotate it further by a small angle d theta. This gives an element of length R times d theta. As theta is increased from zero to pi, the whole wire is covered. <<WRITE_STEP:element length = R d theta, theta from 0 to pi|id=ex-step-1-1>> The coordinates of this element are R cos theta and R sin theta. Since the wire is uniform, the mass per unit length is M divided by pi R. So the mass of the element, d m, equals M over pi R times R d theta, which simplifies to M over pi times d theta. <<WRITE_STEP:element at (R cos theta, R sin theta)|id=ex-step-1-2>> <<WRITE_EQUATION:dm = \frac{M}{\pi R}\,(R\,d\theta) = \frac{M}{\pi}\,d\theta|id=ex-eq-1>> Now we integrate. X is one over M times the integral from zero to pi of R cos theta times M over pi d theta. The integral of cosine over zero to pi vanishes, so X comes out zero. <<WRITE_STEP:X = (1/M) ∫₀^π (R cos theta)(M/pi) d theta = 0|id=ex-step-1-3>> Similarly, Y is one over M times the integral from zero to pi of R sin theta times M over pi d theta. The integral of sine over zero to pi gives two, so Y comes out two R over pi. <<WRITE_STEP:Y = (1/M) ∫₀^π (R sin theta)(M/pi) d theta = 2R/pi|id=ex-step-1-4>> And the answer is: the centre of mass is at zero, two R over pi. Notice it sits on the Y-axis, in empty space off the wire itself. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Centre of mass at (0, 2R/pi)|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter: finding the centre of mass of a uniform semicircular plate. Let the mass of the plate be M and the radius be R. We put the origin at the centre, with the X-axis along the straight edge and the Y-axis in the plane of the plate. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Find centre of mass of a uniform semicircular plate, mass M, radius R|id=ex-q-1>> The trick is to build the plate from nested semicircular wires. Draw a semicircle of radius r and another of radius r plus dr; the element is the ring between radius r and r plus dr. The area of this ring element is pi times r times dr. <<WRITE_STEP:Element = semicircular ring between r and r + dr|id=ex-step-1>> <<WRITE_EQUATION:dA = \pi r\,dr|id=ex-eq-1>> Now the whole area of the plate is pi R squared over two, so the mass per unit area is M divided by pi R squared over two. Multiplying that by the element's area gives the mass of the element as two M r dr over R squared. <<WRITE_STEP:Area of plate = pi R squared over 2, so mass per area = M / (pi R squared / 2)|id=ex-step-2>> <<WRITE_EQUATION:dm = \dfrac{2 M r\,dr}{R^{2}}|id=ex-eq-2>> Each wire element is itself a semicircle, and the centre of mass of each wire is at two r over pi. So we integrate this y-coordinate weighted by the element mass, letting r go from zero to R. <<WRITE_STEP:y of each wire = 2r/pi; integrate r from 0 to R|id=ex-step-3>> <<WRITE_EQUATION:Y = \dfrac{1}{M}\int_{0}^{R}\dfrac{2r}{\pi}\cdot\dfrac{2Mr}{R^{2}}\,dr|id=ex-eq-3>> Working the integral out gives one over M times four M over pi R squared times R cubed over three, and that simplifies to four R over three pi. By symmetry, the x-coordinate is zero. So the centre of mass sits at Y equals four R over three pi. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Y = 4R / (3 pi),  X = 0 by symmetry|id=ex-ans-1>> You've balanced this yourself. Lay a wooden spoon flat across one finger and slide it until it stops tipping. There's exactly one spot where it rests, and for a nice uniform stick that spot sits <<FOCUS:com-point>> right at the middle, at L over two. <<UNFOCUS>> That balance point you found by feel is precisely the centre of mass we just got from slicing the rod into tiny pieces and integrating x times dm. Here's something wild about this. For that semicircular wire, the centre of mass lands at two R over pi, which sits in empty space, completely off the wire itself. <<WRITE_KEY:centre of mass can sit in empty space|id=ext-key-1>> The same thing happens with a boomerang or a curved banana, they spin about a point that isn't even part of the object. That's the whole point of the calculation: the centre of mass is just a weighted average of position, and nothing says that average has to land on the material. <<PAUSE:short>> For a uniform rod the slices are perfectly balanced left and right, so the centre of mass <<FOCUS:com-point>> lands exactly in the middle, right here. <<UNFOCUS>> So a smooth body has no separate weights to add, but by slicing it into infinitely many tiny dm pieces and integrating, we found its balance point anyway.

<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics:centre_of_mass_linear_momentum_collision:9_3>>
<<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:centre_of_mass_linear_momentum_collision:9_3:two_particle_com>> Two particles drift in empty space, far from everything. They pull on each other and start to rush together — but <<FOCUS:com-point>> watch this one point between them. <<FOCUS:particle-a>> Here's particle A and <<FOCUS:particle-b>> the heavier particle B, sitting on a line, and <<FOCUS:com-point>> the centre of mass is this cross — sitting closer to the heavy one, exactly where you'd balance them. <<SECTION:Internal forces|id=sec-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> Now they attract. Particle A <<FOCUS:force-on-a>> feels a force F pulling it toward B, and <<FOCUS:force-on-b>> B feels a force pulling it back toward A — equal in size, opposite in direction. <<UNFOCUS>> These are internal forces — the system tugging on itself. <<WRITE_TEXT:Internal forces come in equal, opposite pairs|id=text-1>> And by Newton's third law they're <<FOCUS:force-on-a+force-on-b>> always exactly equal and opposite. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> So here's the honest question: both particles are accelerating, speeding up, racing toward each other — surely that point between them has to move too? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<ANIMATE_PARAM:t|to=1.0|from=0.0|duration=2500>> Watch carefully as time runs forward — <<FOCUS:particle-a>> A slides right, <<FOCUS:particle-b>> B slides left, they close the gap — and <<FOCUS:com-point>> the cross doesn't budge. The <<FOCUS:com-point+com-guide>> centre of mass stayed frozen, even though both particles moved. <<UNFOCUS>> The reason is what's left when you add up the forces. <<PAUSE:short>> The acceleration of the centre of mass is just the average of the particles' accelerations, weighted by their masses. The acceleration of the centre of mass is the mass-weighted average of the two particles' accelerations. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\vec{a}_{CM} = \dfrac{m_1\vec{a}_1 + m_2\vec{a}_2}{m_1 + m_2}|id=eq-1|boxed>> But A's acceleration is F over m one, and B's is minus F over m two. <<WRITE_STEP:m one times a one equals plus F, m two times a two equals minus F|id=step-1>> When you put these in, m one times its acceleration gives plus F, and m two times its acceleration gives minus F. Plus F and minus F cancel. <<WRITE_KEY:No external force, then the centre of mass never accelerates|id=key-1>> The top is zero, so the acceleration of the centre of mass is zero — no external force means it simply cannot accelerate. <<PAUSE:short>> Put in each acceleration: the plus F from A and the minus F from B cancel exactly, leaving zero on top. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\vec{a}_{CM} = \dfrac{m_1(F/m_1) + m_2(-F/m_2)}{m_1 + m_2} = 0|id=eq-2|boxed>> Here's an example from the chapter. Two charged particles of masses m and two m are placed a distance d apart on a smooth horizontal table, so there's no friction. Because they attract each other, they move towards each other and collide. The question is: where will the collision occur with respect to their initial positions? <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Masses m and 2m, distance d apart on a frictionless table, attract and collide. Where do they collide?|id=ex-q-1>> We start by looking at the external forces. The table is smooth, so the weight of each particle and the normal force balance, since there's no vertical motion. The attraction between the particles is purely internal to the system. So the sum of external forces on the system is zero, which means the centre of mass has no acceleration. <<WRITE_STEP:External force on system = 0, so a of centre of mass = 0|id=ex-step-1-1>> Now both particles start at rest, so the velocity of the centre of mass is zero. With zero acceleration and zero initial velocity, the centre of mass simply never moves. <<WRITE_STEP:Both start at rest, so velocity of centre of mass = 0, centre of mass stays fixed|id=ex-step-1-2>> At the moment of collision, both particles are at one single place, and the centre of mass must also be at that very place. But since the centre of mass hasn't moved at all, the collision happens exactly at the centre of mass. <<WRITE_STEP:At collision both particles coincide with centre of mass, so collision occurs at the centre of mass|id=ex-step-1-3>> Finally we locate that point. The centre of mass sits at a distance two d over three from the initial position of the particle of mass m, toward the other particle. <<WRITE_EQUATION:x_{cm} = \frac{2d}{3}|id=ex-eq-1>> And so the answer is: the collision takes place at the centre of mass, a distance two d over three from the initial position of the particle of mass m, toward the other particle. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Collision occurs at the centre of mass, 2d/3 from the mass m, toward the mass 2m|id=ex-ans-1>> Watch a diver next time the Olympics are on. They leap off the board, fold into a tuck, spin through a couple of somersaults, and slice into the water. Their arms and legs are flying around in wild arcs — but there's one point in their body that doesn't care about any of that. <<WRITE_TEXT:diver's centre of mass = clean parabola|id=ext-1>> The centre of mass traces a single smooth parabola from the board straight down to the water. And that's exactly what we just proved. Once they're airborne, gravity is the only external force acting. All the twisting of the limbs is internal — it can't move the centre of mass off its parabola. The somersaults rearrange the body around that point, but the point itself glides on, as if a single particle had been tossed into the air. Here's something wild to think about the next time you watch fireworks. The shell arcs up into the sky, and then — bang — it bursts into hundreds of sparks flying outward in every direction. But the explosion is entirely an internal force. So even though the sparks scatter everywhere, the centre of mass of that whole glowing cloud keeps gliding along the very same parabola the shell was already following, as if the explosion never happened. The fireworks designers are quietly relying on Newton's third law every single show. If it can't accelerate, its velocity never changes. And since these two started at rest, the centre of mass stays nailed in place — internal forces alone can never shift it. <<PAUSE:short>> That's the deep idea: no matter how violently the parts of a system push and pull each other, only an outside force can move their centre of mass.

<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics:centre_of_mass_linear_momentum_collision:9_4>>
<<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:centre_of_mass_linear_momentum_collision:9_4:recoil_explosion>> A nucleus is sitting perfectly still, then it <<FOCUS:alpha-body>> spits out a tiny alpha particle that goes flying off to the right, so why does the <<FOCUS:nucleus-body>> heavy leftover suddenly start drifting left? <<PAUSE:long>> <<SECTION:Momentum of one particle|id=sec-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> To answer that, start with the simplest thing: a single moving particle carries something physicists call momentum, and it is just how much mass is moving and how fast. The momentum of a single particle is just its mass multiplied by its velocity, and because velocity has a direction, momentum is an arrow too. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\vec{p} = m\vec{v}|id=eq-1|boxed>> Momentum is mass times velocity, and because velocity points in a direction, momentum is an arrow too, pointing exactly the way the particle moves. Now imagine not one particle, but a whole swarm of them, each with its own little momentum arrow, and we simply add all those arrows together to get the total momentum of the system. Here is the beautiful shortcut: when you add up all those individual arrows, the messy sum collapses into <<FOCUS:centre-mass-dot>> one clean statement about the centre of mass. <<UNFOCUS>> Add up the momentum of every particle in a system, and the whole sum collapses to the total mass times the velocity of the centre of mass. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\vec{P} = M\vec{V}_{CM}|id=eq-2|boxed>> <<WRITE_KEY:Total momentum = total mass times velocity of centre of mass|id=key-1>> The total momentum of the whole system equals its total mass times the velocity of its centre of mass, so you never have to track every particle. <<PAUSE:short>> This is powerful because instead of a thousand arrows, the entire system's motion lives in one mass and one velocity — the velocity of the centre of mass. <<PAUSE:short>> <<SECTION:Conservation|id=sec-2>> Now recall what we learned before: if the external forces on a system add up to zero, the centre of mass cannot accelerate at all. If the outside forces add up to zero, the centre of mass cannot accelerate, so the total momentum can never change. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\vec{P} = \text{constant}|id=eq-3|boxed>> <<WRITE_KEY:No external force means total momentum is constant|id=key-2>> If the velocity of the centre of mass never changes, then the total momentum never changes either, no matter what chaos happens inside. <<PAUSE:short>> So back to our still nucleus: before it bursts, nothing is moving, <<FOCUS:centre-mass-dot+cm-label>> the centre of mass is at rest, and the total momentum is exactly zero. <<UNFOCUS>> Here's an example from the chapter. Consider a radioactive nucleus that is initially at rest, and it <<FOCUS:axis>> emits an alpha particle along the X-axis. The alpha particle <<FOCUS:alpha-body>> has mass m and is emitted with speed v, while the <<FOCUS:nucleus-body>> residual nucleus has mass M and recoils with speed V. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: A nucleus at rest emits an alpha particle (mass m, speed v); find the recoil speed V of the residual nucleus (mass M).|id=ex-q-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> We take the entire nucleus as our system. The alpha particle is ejected because of the forces between the neutrons and protons inside, that is, only internal nuclear forces act, and there is no external force on the system. So the total linear momentum cannot change. <<WRITE_STEP:System = whole nucleus; only internal forces, no external force ⇒ momentum conserved|id=ex-step-1-1>> Now, before the emission the nucleus was at rest, so the <<FOCUS:total-momentum-label>> total momentum before emission is zero. <<WRITE_STEP:p_before = 0|id=ex-step-1-2>> <<UNFOCUS>> After the emission, the system breaks into two parts: the alpha particle moving with speed v, and the residual nucleus recoiling with speed V. Setting the total momentum after equal to zero gives M times V plus m times v equals zero. <<WRITE_EQUATION:M V + m v = 0|id=ex-eq-1>> Solving for V, we get V equals minus m over M times v. The minus sign tells us the residual nucleus <<FOCUS:nucleus-momentum-arrow+alpha-momentum-arrow>> recoils in the opposite direction to the alpha particle. <<WRITE_ANSWER:V = - (m/M) v|id=ex-ans-1>> <<PAUSE:short>> There is no external force, so that zero must survive the explosion: the <<FOCUS:alpha-momentum-arrow>> alpha particle shoots right with some momentum, and the leftover nucleus must carry an <<FOCUS:nucleus-momentum-arrow>> equal momentum to the left <<FOCUS:total-momentum-label>> so the two arrows cancel. <<UNFOCUS>> That is why the heavy nucleus recoils: not because something pushed it from outside, but because the total momentum was zero and had to stay zero — conservation of momentum in action. <<PAUSE:short>>

A cricket ball slams into a bat and rockets back the other way in less than one hundredth of a second, so how does such a tiny sliver of time deliver such a brutal kick? <<PAUSE:long>> While the ball and the bat are touching, each one pushes hard on the other, and that push is what flips the ball's motion around. <<SECTION:Impulse and Impulsive Force|id=sec-1>> Here is the surprising part: the contact lasts only a blink, yet the ball's momentum changes by a huge amount. <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:centre_of_mass_linear_momentum_collision:9_11:force_time_curve>> Let's put that push on a graph, with <<FOCUS:force-axis>> force going up the side and <<FOCUS:time-axis>> time running across the bottom. The force isn't steady — it starts at zero, <<TRACE:force-curve>> swells up to an enormous peak, then drops back to zero as the two bodies separate. Notice how narrow this whole event is along the time axis — the entire collision is squeezed into <<FOCUS:contact-interval>> this thin little contact interval. <<WRITE_KEY:Impulse = area under the force-time curve = change in momentum|id=key-1>> Now <<FOCUS:area-shade>> shade in the whole region under the curve — that shaded area is what we call the impulse, and it is exactly equal to the change in momentum. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> The impulse is the total push added up over the contact time, and it equals the final momentum minus the initial momentum. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\vec{J} = \int_{t_i}^{t_f} \vec{F}\,dt = \vec{P}_f - \vec{P}_i|id=eq-1|boxed>> So the impulse is just every little bit of force, added up across the time of contact, and that total equals the final momentum minus the starting momentum. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_TEXT:short time + big momentum change => huge force|id=text-1>>Here's the honest puzzle: if the area stays the same but I make the time interval razor-thin, what has to happen to <<FOCUS:peak-marker>> the height of the curve? <<PAUSE:long>> <<UNFOCUS>> If we squeeze the same change in momentum into a smaller time, the average force has to grow. <<WRITE_EQUATION:F_{avg} = \dfrac{\Delta P}{\Delta t}|id=eq-2|boxed>> <<PAUSE:short>> The curve has no choice but to shoot up — to fit the same area into a sliver of time, the peak force becomes enormous, and <<FOCUS:peak-marker>> that towering peak is the impulsive force. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> This is why a stamping pole-vaulter's pole bends and why airbags exist — stretch the time out and you tame the force, shrink the time and the force turns violent. <<PAUSE:short>> So remember the picture: impulse is the <<FOCUS:area-shade>> area under the force-time curve, it equals the change in momentum, and a short contact time is exactly what makes the impulsive force so huge.

<<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:centre_of_mass_linear_momentum_collision:0_2 m:block_on_ramp_ice>> <<FOCUS:small-block>> A block slides down a curved ramp that's free to roll on frictionless ice — as the block speeds up, why does <<FOCUS:ramp-block>> the ramp glide backwards all on its own? <<PAUSE:long>> <<SECTION:One rule behind every collision|id=sec-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> Here's the secret these problems all share: nobody is pushing the system from outside, sideways, at all. <<PAUSE:short>> The ice is <<FOCUS:ice-surface>> frictionless, so there is no horizontal force from the ground — gravity pulls straight down, and the ice pushes straight up. <<WRITE_KEY:No outside sideways force means total momentum is conserved|id=key-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> And when no outside horizontal force acts, the total momentum of the whole system simply cannot change. <<PAUSE:short>> At the start, everything is at rest, so the total momentum is exactly zero. Now watch the <<FOCUS:block-velocity>> small block slide to the right — it picks up rightward momentum. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> But the total has to stay zero — so something must carry equal momentum the other way. That's why the <<FOCUS:ramp-velocity>> ramp glides backwards on its own. The block's rightward momentum and the ramp's leftward momentum are <<FOCUS:block-velocity+ramp-velocity>> equal and opposite, so they cancel to zero every instant. <<UNFOCUS>> The block's momentum to the right plus the ramp's momentum to the left always add up to zero. <<WRITE_EQUATION:p_{\text{block}} + p_{\text{ramp}} = 0|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<SECTION:The centre of mass barely cares|id=sec-2>> Here's the beautiful twin of that idea: look at the <<FOCUS:com-marker>> centre of mass of the whole system. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Centre of mass keeps moving exactly as before|id=key-2>> Because the total momentum stays zero, the centre of mass never drifts sideways — it <<FOCUS:com-axis>> stays planted right where it began. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> The total momentum of the system stays a fixed constant for as long as no outside sideways force acts. <<WRITE_EQUATION:m_1 v_1 + m_2 v_2 = \text{constant}|id=eq-2|boxed>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Internal pushes cancel in pairs|id=text-1>> The block and ramp push hard on each other, but those are internal forces — they always come in equal, opposite pairs and never move the centre of mass. So whether it's a block on a ramp, two balls colliding, or a particle striking a sphere off-centre, ask the same two questions: is momentum conserved, and where is the centre of mass going? Answer those, and every one of these problems falls open.

topics.our_understanding: This part of the chapter is really just a collection of figures and the answer key for the end-of-chapter problems, so there isn't a fresh concept being taught here with full worked solutions. But let me help you see what these figures and answers are pointing toward, because they tie together everything we've learned about centre of mass, linear momentum, and collisions. Think about what all these problems have in common. In each one, you have objects interacting — a small block sliding over a larger curved block, two balls colliding, a particle striking a sphere off-center. The big idea threaded through all of them is that when no outside horizontal force acts on a system, the total momentum stays the same, and the centre of mass keeps moving exactly as it was. That single principle lets you solve problems that look impossibly complicated. Notice how several of the questions ask about frictionless surfaces. That's a clue. When surfaces are frictionless, the only forces between the blocks are internal pushes, so the horizontal momentum of the whole system is conserved. That's why, in the problem about the small mass sliding on the big curved block, you can find the big block's speed just from momentum, getting that the larger block moves with a speed of m times v divided by the quantity M plus m. Then to find heights and final speeds, you bring in energy conservation, since frictionless means no energy is lost to heat. And look at the lovely result for two equal masses making an elastic collision that isn't head-on — they always fly apart at right angles to each other. That's a surprising and elegant truth that comes purely from combining momentum conservation with kinetic energy conservation. The answer key here is your way to check yourself. When you work through these exercises, you compare your final expression or number to what's listed. If you get the small particle going along the tangent with speed v times rho over r, and the sphere moving perpendicular with speed v over r times the square root of r squared minus rho squared, you know your collision reasoning held together. So treat this section as a map: the figures show the situations, and the answers confirm that conservation of momentum and energy, applied carefully, will get you home.

Solution : 1st collision : As the balls have equal mass and
make elastic collision, the velocities are interchanged.
Hence, after the first collision, the ball A comes to rest
and the ball B moves towards right at a speed v.
2nd collision : The ball B moving with a speed v, collides

ball rebounds at the same speed v towards left.

speed v again collides with the ball A kept at rest. As
the masses are equal and the collision is elastic, the
velocities are interchanged. Thus, the ball B comes to
rest and the ball A moves towards left at a speed v. No
further collision takes place. Thus, the speeds of the
balls remain the same as their initial values.

topics.our_understanding:
This section is a big collection of worked problems all built on one powerful idea: when no outside horizontal force acts on a system, its total linear momentum stays constant. Let me walk you through the thinking. Imagine a boy standing on a board on frictionless ice. When he jumps, he pushes the board backward. Since there was no sideways push from outside, the momentum the boy gains in one direction must be exactly matched by the momentum the board gains in the other. That's why the board recoils, and that's why we can solve for its speed. The same logic appears again and again, just dressed in different clothes. A man walking on a platform, a bullet embedding in a pendulum bob, two blocks pushed apart by a compressed spring — every time, total momentum before equals total momentum after.

Notice that we often combine momentum conservation with two other tools. The first is energy: in elastic collisions kinetic energy is also conserved, and when a spring is involved, the spring's stored energy converts into the kinetic energy of the blocks. The second is the idea of relative velocity. When something moves relative to a moving object, you add velocities carefully. For the space shuttle ejecting a module, the module's speed with respect to earth is its speed relative to the shuttle plus the shuttle's speed relative to earth.

For collisions we also meet the coefficient of restitution, which tells you how bouncy a collision is. It compares the velocity at which two objects separate after the hit to the velocity at which they approached before the hit. When that ratio is one, the collision is perfectly elastic and no kinetic energy is lost. When it's less than one, some energy turns into heat or sound, and we can calculate exactly how much.

A clever trick appears in the spring-and-force problem: we step into the centre of mass frame, where the whole system's centre stays put, and add pseudo forces to account for the acceleration. This lets us find the maximum stretch of a spring using work and energy.

Think of this whole section as a gymnasium for one muscle — momentum conservation — used together with energy ideas and a bit of geometry. Master the pattern of writing momentum before equals momentum after, and these problems become wonderfully repetitive in the best way.

book_examples.verbatim_text: The velocity of the ejected module with respect to the earth = its velocity with respect to the shuttle + the velocity of the shuttle with respect to the earth = −100 km/h + 4000 km/h = 3900 km/h. If the final velocity of the shuttle is V then the total final linear momentum = (5M/6) V + (M/6) × 3900 km/h. By the principle of conservation of linear momentum, M(4000 km/h) = (5M/6) V + (M/6) × 3900 km/h, or V = 4020 km/h.
book_examples.lesson_focus: When part of a moving body is ejected, total momentum is conserved and relative velocities must be added correctly.

remaining shuttle is five sixths of mass M
