final shuttle velocity V = 4020 km/h

book_examples.verbatim_text: 14. A boy of mass 25 kg stands on a board of mass 10 kg which in turn is kept on a frictionless horizontal ice surface. The boy makes a jump with a velocity component 5 m/s in a horizontal direction with respect to the ice. With what velocity does the board recoil? With what rate are the boy and the board separating from each other? Solution: Consider the "board + boy" as a system. The external forces on this system are (a) weight of the system and (b) normal contact force by the ice surface. Both these forces are vertical and there is no external force in horizontal direction. The horizontal component of linear momentum of the "board + boy" system is, therefore, constant. If the board recoils at a speed v, 0 = (25 kg) × (5 m/s) − (10 kg)v, or v = 12.5 m/s. The boy and the board are separating with a rate 5 m/s + 12.5 m/s = 17.5 m/s.
book_examples.lesson_focus: With no horizontal external force, the forward momentum of the boy equals the backward momentum of the board.
setup_facts: boy mass = 25 kg
board mass = 10 kg
ice surface frictionless
boy jumps at 5 m/s horizontal relative to ice
board recoil speed v = 12.5 m/s
separation rate = 17.5 m/s

book_examples.verbatim_text: 15. A man of mass m is standing on a platform of mass M kept on smooth ice. If the man starts moving on the platform with a speed v relative to the platform, with what velocity relative to the ice does the platform recoil? Solution: Suppose the man moves at a speed w towards right and the platform recoils at a speed V towards left, both relative to the ice. Hence, the speed of the man relative to the platform is V + w. By the question, V + w = v, or w = v − V. Taking the platform and the man to be the system, there is no external horizontal force on the system. The linear momentum of the system remains constant. Initially, both the man and the platform were at rest. Thus, 0 = MV − mw or MV = m(v − V), or V = mv/(M + m).
book_examples.lesson_focus: Relative velocity links the man's and platform's speeds, and momentum conservation gives the recoil in terms of masses.
setup_facts: man mass = m
platform mass = M
smooth ice
man moves at speed v relative to platform
both start at rest
platform recoil V = mv divided by (M + m)

book_examples.verbatim_text: 16. A ball of mass m, moving with a velocity v along X-axis, strikes another ball of mass 2m kept at rest. The first ball comes to rest after collision and the other breaks into two equal pieces. One of the pieces starts moving along Y-axis with a speed v1. What will be the velocity of the other piece? Solution: The total linear momentum of the balls before the collision is mv along the X-axis. After the collision, momentum of the first ball = 0, momentum of the first piece = m v1 along the Y-axis and momentum of the second piece = m v2 along its direction of motion. Taking components along the X-axis, m v2 cosθ = m v, and taking components along the Y-axis, m v2 sinθ = m v1. From these, v2 = √(v² + v1²) and tanθ = v1/v.
book_examples.lesson_focus: Momentum is a vector, so it must be conserved separately along each axis.
setup_facts: first ball mass = m, velocity v along X-axis
second ball mass = 2m at rest
first ball stops after collision
second ball breaks into two equal pieces of mass m each
one piece moves along Y-axis at speed v1
other piece speed v2 = square root of (v squared plus v1 squared)
tan theta = v1 over v

book_examples.verbatim_text: 17. A bullet of mass 50 g is fired from below into the bob of mass 450 g of a long simple pendulum. The bullet remains inside the bob and the bob rises through a height of 1.8 m. Find the speed of the bullet. Take g = 10 m/s². Solution: Let the speed of the bullet be v. Let the common velocity of the bullet and the bob, after the bullet is embedded into the bob, is V. By the principle of conservation of linear momentum, V = (0.05 kg)v / (0.45 kg + 0.05 kg) = v/10. The string becomes loose and the bob will go up with a deceleration of g = 10 m/s². As it comes to rest at a height of 1.8 m, using the equation v² = u² − 2ax, 1.8 m = (v/10)² / (2 × 10 m/s²), or v = 60 m/s.
book_examples.lesson_focus: A ballistic pendulum combines inelastic momentum conservation with energy or kinematics for the rise.
setup_facts: bullet mass = 50 g = 0.05 kg
bob mass = 450 g = 0.45 kg
bullet embeds in bob
common velocity V = v/10
bob rises 1.8 m
g = 10 m/s²
bullet speed v = 60 m/s

book_examples.verbatim_text: 18. A light spring of spring constant k is kept compressed between two blocks of masses m and M on a smooth horizontal surface. When released, the blocks acquire velocities in opposite directions. The spring loses contact with the blocks when it acquires natural length. If the spring was initially compressed through a distance x, find the final speeds of the two blocks. Solution: Consider the two blocks plus the spring to be the system. No external force acts horizontally, so linear momentum is constant. As the spring is light, it has no linear momentum. Suppose block M moves at speed V and the other block at speed v. Initial momentum is zero, so MV − mv = 0, or V = (m/M)v. Initially the energy is (1/2)kx². Finally it is (1/2)mv² + (1/2)MV². With no friction, (1/2)mv² + (1/2)MV² = (1/2)kx². Using these, v = √(kM / (m(M+m))) x and V = √(km / (M(M+m))) x.
book_examples.lesson_focus: A released compressed spring conserves both momentum (zero total) and energy (stored spring energy becomes kinetic).
setup_facts: blocks of masses m and M
light spring constant k
smooth horizontal surface
initial compression = x
both start at rest, momentum zero
M moves at V, other at v, with V = (m/M)v
spring energy = one half k x squared
final speed v = square root of (k M divided by m times (M plus m)) times x
final speed V = square root of (k m divided by M times (M plus m)) times x

book_examples.verbatim_text: 19. A block of mass m is connected to another block of mass M by a massless spring of spring constant k. The blocks are kept on a smooth horizontal plane. Initially the blocks are at rest and the spring is unstretched when a constant force F starts acting on the block of mass M to pull it. Find the maximum extension of the spring. Solution: Take the two blocks plus the spring as the system. The centre of mass moves with acceleration a = F/(m+M). Work from a reference frame at the centre of mass, applying pseudo forces. The net external force on m is F1 = ma = mF/(m+M) towards left, and on M is F2 = F − Ma = mF/(m+M) towards right. The blocks come to instantaneous rest at maximum extension. The total work done by F1 and F2 is W = (mF/(m+M))(x1 + x2). This equals the increase in spring potential energy: (mF/(m+M))(x1+x2) = (1/2)k(x1+x2)². So x1 + x2 = 2mF / (k(m+M)). This is the maximum extension.
book_examples.lesson_focus: Working in the centre of mass frame with pseudo forces, the work done equals the spring's stored energy at maximum extension.
setup_facts: blocks of masses m and M joined by spring constant k
smooth horizontal plane
constant force F pulls block M
both start at rest, spring unstretched
centre of mass acceleration a = F divided by (m plus M)
effective force on each block = m F divided by (m plus M)
maximum extension = 2 m F divided by k times (m plus M)

book_examples.verbatim_text: 20. Two identical balls, the first moving at speed v towards right and the second at rest, with a fixed wall at the extreme right. Assume all collisions elastic. Show that the speeds of the balls remain unchanged after all collisions. Solution: 1st collision: equal masses making elastic collision interchange velocities, so ball A comes to rest and ball B moves right at speed v. 2nd collision: ball B collides with the rigid wall (infinite mass) and rebounds at the same speed v towards left, since velocity of separation equals velocity of approach. 3rd collision: ball B moving left at speed v collides with ball A at rest; equal masses, elastic, so velocities interchange. Ball B comes to rest and ball A moves left at speed v. No further collision. Thus the speeds remain the same as their initial values.
book_examples.lesson_focus: In elastic collisions between equal masses velocities are exchanged, and an infinite-mass wall just reverses velocity.
setup_facts: two identical balls A and B
ball A moving right at speed v, ball B at rest
fixed wall at extreme right
all collisions elastic
equal masses exchange velocities
wall reverses ball's velocity at same speed
final speeds unchanged from initial

book_examples.verbatim_text: 21. A block of mass m moving at a velocity v collides head on with another block of mass 2m at rest. If the coefficient of restitution is 1/2, find the velocities of the blocks after the collision. Solution: Suppose after the collision the block of mass m moves at velocity u1 and the block of mass 2m moves at velocity u2. By conservation of momentum, mv = mu1 + 2mu2. The velocity of separation is u2 − u1 and the velocity of approach is v, so u2 − u1 = v/2. From these, u1 = 0 and u2 = v/2.
book_examples.lesson_focus: Combining momentum conservation with the restitution equation solves a non-elastic head-on collision.
setup_facts: block mass m at velocity v
block mass 2m at rest
head-on collision
coefficient of restitution = 1/2

book_examples.verbatim_text: 22. A block of mass 1.2 kg moving at a speed of 20 cm/s collides head-on with a similar block kept at rest. The coefficient of restitution is 3/5. Find the loss of kinetic energy during the collision. Solution: Suppose the first block moves at v1 and the second at v2 after collision. By conservation of momentum, 1.2 kg × 20 cm/s = 1.2 kg × v1 + 1.2 kg × v2, or v1 + v2 = 20 cm/s. The velocity of separation is v2 − v1 and velocity of approach is 20 cm/s, so v2 − v1 = (3/5)(20 cm/s) = 12 cm/s. From these, v1 = 4 cm/s and v2 = 16 cm/s. The loss in kinetic energy is (1/2)(1.2 kg)[(20 cm/s)² − (4 cm/s)² − (16 cm/s)²] = 0.6 kg × 0.0128 m²/s² = 7.7 × 10⁻³ J.
book_examples.lesson_focus: After finding final velocities, the kinetic energy lost in an inelastic collision can be computed directly.
setup_facts: both blocks mass 1.2 kg
first block speed 20 cm/s, second at rest
coefficient of restitution = 3/5
v1 = 4 cm/s, v2 = 16 cm/s
loss of kinetic energy = 7.7 times ten to the minus three joules

book_examples.verbatim_text: 23. A ball of mass m hits the floor with a speed v making an angle of incidence θ with the normal. The coefficient of restitution is e. Find the speed of the reflected ball and the angle of reflection. Solution: Suppose the angle of reflection is θ' and the speed after collision is v'. The floor exerts force only along the normal, so the parallel component of velocity is unchanged: v' sinθ' = v sinθ. For the normal components, velocity of separation = v' cosθ' and velocity of approach = v cosθ, so v' cosθ' = e v cosθ. From these, v' = v√(sin²θ + e²cos²θ) and tanθ' = tanθ/e. For elastic collision, e = 1 so θ' = θ and v' = v.
book_examples.lesson_focus: Only the normal component of velocity is affected by restitution; the tangential component stays the same.
setup_facts: ball mass m, speed v, angle of incidence theta with normal
coefficient of restitution e
tangential velocity unchanged: v prime sin theta prime = v sin theta
normal velocity: v prime cos theta prime = e v cos theta
reflected speed v prime = v times square root of (sine squared theta plus e squared cosine squared theta)
tan theta prime = tan theta divided by e

book_examples.verbatim_text: 24. A block of mass m and a pan of equal mass are connected by a string over a smooth light pulley. Initially the system is at rest when a particle of mass m falls on the pan and sticks to it. If the particle strikes the pan with a speed v find the speed with which the system moves just after the collision. Solution: Let the required speed be V. Let N be the contact force between particle and pan, T the tension. The impulse on the particle: ∫N dt = mv − mV. The impulse on the pan: ∫(N − T)dt = mV. The impulse on the block: ∫T dt = mV. Adding the last two, ∫N dt = 2mV. Comparing with the first, mv − mV = 2mV, so V = v/3.
book_examples.lesson_focus: Using impulse equations for each part of a connected system gives the common speed after a sticking collision.
setup_facts: block mass m and pan mass m over smooth light pulley
system initially at rest
particle of mass m falls and sticks to pan
particle strikes pan at speed v
common speed after collision V = v/3

events.text: Boy's forward momentum is cancelled by the board's backward momentum
Total momentum before = total momentum after = 0
Q: Shuttle at 4000 km/h ejects 1/6 of its mass backward at 100 km/h relative to shuttle. Find final shuttle speed V.
module velocity (rel. earth) = -100 + 4000 = 3900 km/h
V = 4020 km/h
Q: Boy 25 kg on board 10 kg on frictionless ice; boy jumps at 5 m/s. Find board recoil and separation rate.
System = board + boy; no horizontal external force, so horizontal momentum is conserved.
Board recoil v = 12.5 m/s; separation rate = 5 + 12.5 = 17.5 m/s
Q: Man (mass m) on platform (mass M) on smooth ice; man moves at speed v relative to platform. Find platform recoil V relative to ice.
V + w = v, so w = v − V
0 = MV − mw
MV = m(v − V) → V(M + m) = mv
V = mv / (M + m)
Q: Mass m at velocity v hits mass 2m at rest; first stops, 2m splits into two equal pieces m each; one piece moves along Y at v1. Find the other piece's velocity.
Before: p = m v along X-axis
After: first ball 0; piece 1 = m v1 along Y; piece 2 = m v2 at angle theta
X-axis: m v2 cos(theta) = m v
Y-axis: m v2 sin(theta) = m v1
Square and add: v2^2 = v^2 + v1^2
Divide: tan(theta) = v1 / v
v2 = sqrt(v^2 + v1^2), at angle theta with tan(theta) = v1/v
Q: Bullet (0.05 kg) embeds in bob (0.45 kg); bob rises 1.8 m. Find bullet speed. g = 10 m/s^2
v = 60 m/s
Q: Spring (constant k) compressed by x between blocks m and M on a smooth surface, released from rest. Find final speeds.
M V − m v = 0  ⟹  V = (m/M) v
½ m v² + ½ M V² = ½ k x²
Substitute V = (m/M)v, then solve for v
Q: Blocks m and M joined by spring k on smooth plane; constant force F pulls M from rest. Find max extension.
Take system = both blocks + spring; centre of mass acceleration a = F / (m + M)
Effective force on each block = mF / (m + M)
Maximum extension = 2mF / (k(m + M))
Q: Ball A moves right at v, ball B at rest, fixed wall at right, all collisions elastic. Show final speeds unchanged.
Final speeds unchanged: both balls move at speed v, same as initial.
Q: mass m at velocity v hits mass 2m at rest head-on, restitution = 1/2; find final velocities
m v = m u1 + 2m u2
v = u1 + 2u2, with u2 = u1 + v/2
Q: 1.2 kg block at 20 cm/s hits identical block at rest, e = 3/5. Find KE lost.
v1 = 4 cm/s,  v2 = 16 cm/s
Loss of KE = 7.7 × 10⁻³ J
Q: Ball of mass m hits floor at speed v, angle theta with normal, restitution e. Find reflected speed and angle.
v' sin(theta') = v sin(theta)
v' cos(theta') = e v cos(theta)
v' = v * sqrt(sin^2(theta) + e^2 cos^2(theta))
v' = v*sqrt(sin^2(theta) + e^2 cos^2(theta)),  tan(theta') = tan(theta)/e
Q: Block (m) and pan (m) over a smooth light pulley, at rest. Particle (m) hits the pan at speed v and sticks. Find the speed V just after collision.
Particle: ∫N dt = mv − mV
Pan: ∫(N − T) dt = mV
Block: ∫T dt = mV
Add pan + block: ∫N dt = 2mV
Compare: mv − mV = 2mV → mv = 3mV
V = v/3
step off canoe, boat recoils

topics.standalone_narration_text: <<FOCUS:board>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:centre_of_mass_linear_momentum_collision:2_2 m:boy_board_ice>> A boy stands perfectly still on a board, on ice so slippery there's no friction at all. He bends his knees and jumps forward. The board shoots backward. But nothing outside touched it, so where did that motion come from? <<PAUSE:long>> <<FOCUS:system-dashed-box>> Here's the secret. Watch the boy and the board not as two separate things, but as one team inside this dashed box. <<FOCUS:ice-surface>> <<SECTION:The recoil idea|id=sec-1>>The only outside forces are gravity pulling down and the ice pushing up. Both point straight up and down. Sideways, there is nothing pushing this team at all. <<FOCUS:system-dashed-box>> And here is the rule that makes everything click: when no outside sideways push acts on a system, the total sideways momentum stays exactly the same as it was before. <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:boy>> Before the jump, nobody is moving. The total momentum is zero. So after the jump, the total must still be zero. That's the question we have to answer: how can things move, yet add up to zero? <<PAUSE:long>> <<FOCUS:boy-momentum-arrow>> The boy launches forward, so he carries momentum that way. <<TRACE:boy-momentum-arrow>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:board-momentum-arrow>> <<WRITE_KEY:Boy's forward momentum is cancelled by the board's backward momentum|id=key-1>>For the total to stay zero, the board must carry exactly the same amount of momentum the other way. The two arrows are the same length, pointing opposite. Add them, and they cancel to zero. That's your payoff: the board moves because it has to, to keep the books balanced. <<TRACE:board-momentum-arrow>> <<PAUSE:short>> Now momentum is mass times velocity. So a heavy board needs only a small speed to match a lighter boy moving fast. The lighter you are, the faster you recoil. <<POINT:board-momentum-arrow>> <<FOCUS:system-dashed-box>> <<WRITE_STEP:Total momentum before = total momentum after = 0|id=step-1>>Written as an equation, the boy's momentum forward minus the board's momentum backward equals zero, because that's what it was before. <<PAUSE:short>> The total momentum the moment before the jump equals the total momentum the moment after. <<WRITE_EQUATION:p_{\text{before}} = p_{\text{after}}|id=eq-1|boxed>> Rearrange that and you can solve for the board's recoil speed from the boy's mass, the boy's speed, and the board's mass alone. No outside force needed in the maths at all. The boy's mass times his speed equals the board's mass times its recoil speed, so the heavier board moves slower. <<WRITE_EQUATION:m_{\text{boy}} v_{\text{boy}} = m_{\text{board}} v_{\text{board}}|id=eq-2|boxed>> Here's an example from the chapter. A space shuttle is moving at four thousand kilometers per hour relative to the earth. It ejects a module that is one sixth of the total mass M, while the remaining shuttle is five sixths of the mass M. The module is shot out at one hundred kilometers per hour backward relative to the shuttle, and we want the final speed of the shuttle. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Shuttle at 4000 km/h ejects 1/6 of its mass backward at 100 km/h relative to shuttle. Find final shuttle speed V.|id=ex-q-1>> We start by finding the velocity of the ejected module with respect to the earth. That equals its velocity with respect to the shuttle plus the velocity of the shuttle with respect to the earth. So that is minus one hundred kilometers per hour plus four thousand kilometers per hour, which gives three thousand nine hundred kilometers per hour. <<WRITE_STEP:module velocity (rel. earth) = -100 + 4000 = 3900 km/h|id=ex-step-1-1>> Now we apply conservation of linear momentum. If the final velocity of the shuttle is V, then the total final momentum is five sixths M times V plus one sixth M times three thousand nine hundred kilometers per hour. The initial momentum was M times four thousand kilometers per hour. <<WRITE_STEP:M(4000) = (5M/6)V + (M/6)(3900)|id=ex-step-1-2>> The mass M cancels throughout. Solving for V, we rearrange to get five sixths V equals four thousand minus one sixth times three thousand nine hundred, and that gives V equals four thousand and twenty kilometers per hour. <<WRITE_STEP:(5/6)V = 4000 - (1/6)(3900)  =>  V = 4020 km/h|id=ex-step-1-3>> And the answer is that the final velocity of the shuttle is four thousand and twenty kilometers per hour. <<WRITE_ANSWER:V = 4020 km/h|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter. A boy of mass twenty-five kilograms stands on a board of mass ten kilograms, which rests on a frictionless horizontal ice surface. The boy jumps off with a velocity component of five meters per second in the horizontal direction relative to the ice. We want to find the velocity at which the board recoils, and the rate at which the boy and the board separate. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Boy 25 kg on board 10 kg on frictionless ice; boy jumps at 5 m/s. Find board recoil and separation rate.|id=ex-q-1>> We take the board plus boy as one system. The only external forces are the weight of the system and the normal contact force from the ice, and both of these are vertical. Since there is no external force in the horizontal direction, the horizontal component of the system's linear momentum stays constant. Everything starts from rest, so that total horizontal momentum is zero. <<WRITE_STEP:System = board + boy; no horizontal external force, so horizontal momentum is conserved.|id=ex-step-1-1>> Let the board recoil at a speed v. The boy carries momentum twenty-five kilograms times five meters per second forward, and the board carries ten kilograms times v backward. Setting the total to zero gives: zero equals twenty-five kilograms times five meters per second, minus ten kilograms times v. <<WRITE_STEP:0 = (25 kg)(5 m/s) - (10 kg)v|id=ex-step-1-2>> Solving for v, we get ten times v equals one hundred twenty-five, so v equals twelve point five meters per second. That's the board's recoil speed. <<WRITE_STEP:10v = 125, so v = 12.5 m/s|id=ex-step-1-3>> Finally, the boy and the board move in opposite directions, so their separation rate is the sum of their speeds: five meters per second plus twelve point five meters per second, which is seventeen point five meters per second. The board recoils at twelve point five meters per second, and the two separate at seventeen point five meters per second. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Board recoil v = 12.5 m/s; separation rate = 5 + 12.5 = 17.5 m/s|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter. A man of mass m is standing on a platform of mass M, and the platform rests on smooth ice. The man starts moving on the platform with a speed v relative to the platform. Both start at rest. The question is: with what velocity does the platform recoil relative to the ice? <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Man (mass m) on platform (mass M) on smooth ice; man moves at speed v relative to platform. Find platform recoil V relative to ice.|id=ex-q-1>> We start by naming the speeds relative to the ice. Suppose the man moves at speed w toward the right, and the platform recoils at speed V toward the left. The man's speed relative to the platform is then V plus w. Since that relative speed is given as v, we get V plus w equals v, so w equals v minus V. <<WRITE_STEP:V + w = v, so w = v − V|id=ex-step-1-1>> Now take the man and the platform together as one system. The ice is smooth, so there is no external horizontal force on the system, which means the linear momentum stays constant. Both started at rest, so the initial momentum is zero. That gives zero equals M times V minus m times w. <<WRITE_STEP:0 = MV − mw|id=ex-step-1-2>> Substituting w equals v minus V, we get M times V equals m times the quantity v minus V. Expanding and collecting the V terms, M times V plus m times V equals m times v, so V times the quantity M plus m equals m times v. <<WRITE_STEP:MV = m(v − V) → V(M + m) = mv|id=ex-step-1-3>> And the answer is: the platform recoils at a velocity V equal to m times v divided by the quantity M plus m, relative to the ice. <<WRITE_ANSWER:V = mv / (M + m)|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter. A ball of mass m, moving with velocity v along the X-axis, strikes another ball of mass two m kept at rest. The first ball comes to rest after the collision, and the second ball breaks into two equal pieces, each of mass m. One of the pieces starts moving along the Y-axis with a speed v one. We want the velocity of the other piece. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Mass m at velocity v hits mass 2m at rest; first stops, 2m splits into two equal pieces m each; one piece moves along Y at v1. Find the other piece's velocity.|id=ex-q-1>> We start with momentum. Before the collision, the only moving ball is the first one, so the total linear momentum is m times v, directed along the X-axis. After the collision the first ball is at rest, so its momentum is zero. The first piece carries momentum m times v one along the Y-axis, and the second piece carries momentum m times v two along its own direction of motion, at some angle theta. <<WRITE_STEP:Before: p = m v along X-axis|id=ex-step-1-1>><<WRITE_STEP:After: first ball 0; piece 1 = m v1 along Y; piece 2 = m v2 at angle theta|id=ex-step-1-2>> Now we use that momentum is a vector, conserved separately along each axis. Taking components along the X-axis, the second piece must supply all the original X-momentum, so m v two cosine theta equals m v. Taking components along the Y-axis, the second piece must cancel the first piece, so m v two sine theta equals m v one. <<WRITE_STEP:X-axis: m v2 cos(theta) = m v|id=ex-step-1-3>><<WRITE_STEP:Y-axis: m v2 sin(theta) = m v1|id=ex-step-1-4>> Squaring and adding these two equations eliminates theta, giving v two equals the square root of v squared plus v one squared. And dividing the Y equation by the X equation gives tangent theta equals v one over v. <<WRITE_STEP:Square and add: v2^2 = v^2 + v1^2|id=ex-step-1-5>><<WRITE_STEP:Divide: tan(theta) = v1 / v|id=ex-step-1-6>> And the answer is that the other piece moves with speed v two equal to the square root of v squared plus v one squared, in a direction making an angle theta with the X-axis where tangent theta equals v one over v. <<WRITE_ANSWER:v2 = sqrt(v^2 + v1^2), at angle theta with tan(theta) = v1/v|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter, a ballistic pendulum problem. A bullet of mass fifty grams, that's zero point zero five kilograms, is fired from below into the bob of a long simple pendulum. The bob has mass four hundred fifty grams, or zero point four five kilograms. The bullet remains embedded inside the bob, and the bob then rises through a height of one point eight meters. Take g equal to ten meters per second squared. We need to find the speed of the bullet. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Bullet (0.05 kg) embeds in bob (0.45 kg); bob rises 1.8 m. Find bullet speed. g = 10 m/s^2|id=ex-q-1>> We start with the collision itself. Let the speed of the bullet be v. The bullet embeds in the bob, so this is a perfectly inelastic collision, and we use conservation of linear momentum. The bullet's momentum before equals the combined momentum just after. So the common velocity V equals zero point zero five kilograms times v, divided by zero point four five kilograms plus zero point zero five kilograms. That gives us V equals v over ten. <<WRITE_STEP:V = (0.05 v) / (0.45 + 0.05) = v/10|id=ex-step-1-1>> Now the string becomes loose and the bob rises with the combined velocity V. As it goes up, gravity decelerates it at ten meters per second squared, and it comes to rest at a height of one point eight meters. We use the kinematics equation, v squared equals u squared minus two a x. At the top the bob is at rest, so we get one point eight meters equals V squared over two times ten meters per second squared. <<WRITE_STEP:1.8 = V^2 / (2 x 10), with V = v/10|id=ex-step-1-2>> Substituting V equals v over ten, we have one point eight equals v over ten, squared, divided by twenty. Solving for v, we find the bullet's speed. <<WRITE_STEP:1.8 = (v/10)^2 / 20  =>  v = 60|id=ex-step-1-3>> And the answer is sixty meters per second. <<WRITE_ANSWER:v = 60 m/s|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter. A light spring of spring constant k is kept compressed between two blocks of masses m and M on a smooth horizontal surface. The spring is initially compressed through a distance x, and both blocks start at rest, so the total momentum is zero. When released, the blocks fly off in opposite directions. We want the final speeds of the two blocks. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Spring (constant k) compressed by x between blocks m and M on a smooth surface, released from rest. Find final speeds.|id=ex-q-1>> We take the two blocks plus the spring as our system. No external force acts horizontally, so linear momentum is conserved. The spring is light, so it carries no momentum. Suppose block M moves at speed V and the other block at speed v. Since the initial momentum is zero, M times V minus m times v equals zero, which gives V equals m over M times v. <<WRITE_STEP:M V − m v = 0  ⟹  V = (m/M) v|id=ex-step-1>> Now for energy. Initially the energy is just the stored spring energy, one half k x squared. Finally it's the kinetic energy of the two blocks, one half m v squared plus one half M V squared. With no friction, energy is conserved, so one half m v squared plus one half M V squared equals one half k x squared. <<WRITE_STEP:½ m v² + ½ M V² = ½ k x²|id=ex-step-2>> We substitute V equals m over M times v into the energy equation, and solve for v. Working through the algebra gives the two final speeds. <<WRITE_STEP:Substitute V = (m/M)v, then solve for v|id=ex-step-3>> And the answer is: the smaller block's speed v equals the square root of k M divided by m times the quantity M plus m, all times x. And block M's speed V equals the square root of k m divided by M times the quantity M plus m, all times x. <<WRITE_ANSWER:v = √(kM / (m(M+m))) · x ,  V = √(km / (M(M+m))) · x|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter. A block of mass m is connected to another block of mass M by a massless spring of spring constant k, resting on a smooth horizontal plane. Both blocks start at rest with the spring unstretched, and then a constant force F starts acting on the block of mass M to pull it. We want the maximum extension of the spring. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Blocks m and M joined by spring k on smooth plane; constant force F pulls M from rest. Find max extension.|id=ex-q-1>> Take the two blocks plus the spring as one system. The centre of mass moves with acceleration a equals F divided by the quantity m plus M. We'll work in the reference frame of the centre of mass and apply pseudo forces. <<WRITE_STEP:Take system = both blocks + spring; centre of mass acceleration a = F / (m + M)|id=ex-step-1-1>> In this frame, the net external force on m comes out to m F divided by the quantity m plus M, pointing towards the left. And on M, the net force is F minus M times a, which also simplifies to m F divided by the quantity m plus M, pointing towards the right. So each block feels the same effective force, m F divided by m plus M. <<WRITE_STEP:Effective force on each block = mF / (m + M)|id=ex-step-1-2>> The blocks come to instantaneous rest at maximum extension. The total work done by these two forces is m F divided by m plus M, times the sum of the two displacements, x one plus x two. By the work energy idea this equals the increase in the spring's potential energy, one half k times x one plus x two, all squared. <<WRITE_STEP:(mF/(m+M))(x1 + x2) = (1/2) k (x1 + x2)^2|id=ex-step-1-3>> Cancelling one factor of x one plus x two from both sides and solving, the maximum extension is two m F divided by k times the quantity m plus M. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Maximum extension = 2mF / (k(m + M))|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter. We have two identical balls, A and B. Ball A is moving to the right at speed v, while ball B is at rest. At the extreme right there's a fixed wall, and we'll assume all collisions are elastic. The goal is to show that the speeds of the balls remain unchanged after all the collisions. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Ball A moves right at v, ball B at rest, fixed wall at right, all collisions elastic. Show final speeds unchanged.|id=ex-q-1>> First collision: ball A hits ball B. These are equal masses making an elastic collision, and the key fact is that equal masses exchange velocities. So ball A comes to rest, and ball B moves to the right at speed v. <<WRITE_STEP:1st collision: A and B, equal masses, elastic -> exchange velocities. A stops, B moves right at v.|id=ex-step-1-1>> Second collision: ball B now strikes the fixed wall. The wall behaves like an infinite mass, so it reverses the ball's velocity at the same speed. Velocity of separation equals velocity of approach, so ball B rebounds at the same speed v, now moving to the left. <<WRITE_STEP:2nd collision: B hits wall (infinite mass) -> velocity reversed. B moves left at v.|id=ex-step-1-2>> Third collision: ball B, moving left at speed v, collides with ball A, which is at rest. Again equal masses and elastic, so velocities interchange. Ball B comes to rest and ball A moves to the left at speed v. After this there are no further collisions. <<WRITE_STEP:3rd collision: B (left at v) hits A at rest -> exchange velocities. B stops, A moves left at v.|id=ex-step-1-3>> And the answer is that the final speeds are unchanged from the initial values: each ball ends up moving at speed v, exactly as it started. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Final speeds unchanged: both balls move at speed v, same as initial.|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter. A block of mass m moving at a velocity v collides head on with another block of mass two m that's at rest. The coefficient of restitution for this collision is one half, and we want to find the velocities of both blocks after they collide. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: mass m at velocity v hits mass 2m at rest head-on, restitution = 1/2; find final velocities|id=ex-q-1>> We start with conservation of momentum. Suppose after the collision the block of mass m moves at velocity u one, and the block of mass two m moves at velocity u two. Then the total momentum before equals the total momentum after, so m times v equals m times u one plus two m times u two. <<WRITE_STEP:m v = m u1 + 2m u2|id=ex-step-1-1>> Now we use the restitution equation. The velocity of separation is u two minus u one, and the velocity of approach is just v. Since the coefficient of restitution is one half, the velocity of separation equals one half times the velocity of approach, which gives u two minus u one equals v over two. <<WRITE_STEP:u2 - u1 = v/2|id=ex-step-1-2>> Now we solve these two equations together. Cancelling m from the momentum equation gives v equals u one plus two u two, and from the restitution equation u two equals u one plus v over two. Substituting and simplifying, we find u one comes out to zero and u two comes out to v over two. <<WRITE_STEP:v = u1 + 2u2, with u2 = u1 + v/2|id=ex-step-1-3>><<WRITE_STEP:u1 = 0, u2 = v/2|id=ex-step-1-4>> And the answer is: after the collision the block of mass m comes to rest, with u one equal to zero, while the block of mass two m moves off at velocity v over two. <<WRITE_ANSWER:u1 = 0, u2 = v/2|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter. A block of mass one point two kilograms moving at a speed of twenty centimeters per second collides head-on with a similar block of mass one point two kilograms kept at rest. The coefficient of restitution is three-fifths. We want to find the loss of kinetic energy during the collision. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: 1.2 kg block at 20 cm/s hits identical block at rest, e = 3/5. Find KE lost.|id=ex-q-1>> We start with conservation of momentum. Before the collision only the first block moves, so one point two kilograms times twenty centimeters per second equals one point two kilograms times v1 plus one point two kilograms times v2. Since the masses are equal, this simplifies to v1 plus v2 equals twenty centimeters per second. <<WRITE_STEP:1.2(20) = 1.2 v1 + 1.2 v2  →  v1 + v2 = 20 cm/s|id=ex-step-1-1>> Now we use the coefficient of restitution. The velocity of separation, v2 minus v1, equals the restitution times the velocity of approach. So v2 minus v1 equals three-fifths times twenty centimeters per second, which is twelve centimeters per second. <<WRITE_STEP:v2 - v1 = (3/5)(20) = 12 cm/s|id=ex-step-1-2>> Solving these two equations together, we add and subtract them to get v1 equals four centimeters per second and v2 equals sixteen centimeters per second. <<WRITE_STEP:v1 = 4 cm/s,  v2 = 16 cm/s|id=ex-step-1-3>> Now the loss in kinetic energy is one half times one point two kilograms times the quantity twenty squared minus four squared minus sixteen squared, all in centimeters per second. Working that out gives zero point six kilograms times zero point zero one two eight meters squared per second squared. <<WRITE_STEP:ΔKE = (1/2)(1.2)[20² - 4² - 16²] = 0.6 × 0.0128|id=ex-step-1-4>> And the answer is the loss of kinetic energy equals seven point seven times ten to the minus three joules. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Loss of KE = 7.7 × 10⁻³ J|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter. A ball of mass m hits the floor with a speed v, making an angle of incidence theta with the normal, and the coefficient of restitution is e. We need to find the speed of the reflected ball and the angle of reflection. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Ball of mass m hits floor at speed v, angle theta with normal, restitution e. Find reflected speed and angle.|id=ex-q-1>> Let the angle of reflection be theta prime and the speed after collision be v prime. Now the key idea: the floor only exerts a force along the normal, so the component of velocity parallel to the floor, the tangential component, is completely unchanged. That gives us v prime sine theta prime equals v sine theta. <<WRITE_STEP:v' sin(theta') = v sin(theta)|id=ex-step-1-1>> For the normal direction, restitution does its work. The velocity of separation is v prime cosine theta prime and the velocity of approach is v cosine theta, so the normal component obeys v prime cosine theta prime equals e times v cosine theta. <<WRITE_STEP:v' cos(theta') = e v cos(theta)|id=ex-step-1-2>> Now we square both equations and add them. The sine squared plus cosine squared on the left collapses to v prime squared, and we get the reflected speed v prime equals v times the square root of sine squared theta plus e squared cosine squared theta. <<WRITE_STEP:v' = v * sqrt(sin^2(theta) + e^2 cos^2(theta))|id=ex-step-1-3>> And dividing the first equation by the second, the v prime and theta prime terms give us tangent theta prime equals tangent theta divided by e. So the reflected speed is v times the square root of sine squared theta plus e squared cosine squared theta, and the angle of reflection satisfies tangent theta prime equals tangent theta over e. <<WRITE_ANSWER:v' = v*sqrt(sin^2(theta) + e^2 cos^2(theta)),  tan(theta') = tan(theta)/e|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter. A block of mass m and a pan of equal mass m are connected by a string over a smooth, light pulley. The system is initially at rest, when a particle of mass m falls onto the pan and sticks to it. The particle strikes the pan with speed v, and we want the common speed with which the whole system moves just after the collision. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Block (m) and pan (m) over a smooth light pulley, at rest. Particle (m) hits the pan at speed v and sticks. Find the speed V just after collision.|id=ex-q-1>> Let the required common speed be capital V. During the brief collision, let capital N be the contact force between the particle and the pan, and capital T the string tension. We write the impulse on each part. For the particle, the impulse from the contact force slows it from v down to V, so the integral of N with respect to time equals m v minus m capital V. <<WRITE_STEP:Particle: ∫N dt = mv − mV|id=ex-step-1-1>> Now the pan. The pan feels the contact force N pushing it down and the tension T pulling it up, and it speeds up from rest to capital V, so the integral of N minus T with respect to time equals m capital V. And the block, pulled by the same tension, also reaches capital V, so the integral of T with respect to time equals m capital V. <<WRITE_STEP:Pan: ∫(N − T) dt = mV|id=ex-step-1-2>><<WRITE_STEP:Block: ∫T dt = mV|id=ex-step-1-3>> Adding the pan and block equations, the tension impulses cancel, so the integral of N with respect to time equals two m capital V. Comparing this with the particle equation, m v minus m capital V equals two m capital V. <<WRITE_STEP:Add pan + block: ∫N dt = 2mV|id=ex-step-1-4>><<WRITE_STEP:Compare: mv − mV = 2mV → mv = 3mV|id=ex-step-1-5>> Cancelling the mass m and solving, three capital V equals v, so capital V equals v over three. The system moves just after the collision with speed v divided by three. <<WRITE_ANSWER:V = v/3|id=ex-ans-1>> You've felt this yourself in a small boat or canoe. The instant you push forward to step onto the dock, the boat scoots backward under your feet, and suddenly you're reaching for something to grab. That's not clumsiness, that's momentum conservation. With the water giving almost no sideways grip, the forward momentum you gain has to be paid for by an equal and opposite momentum given to the boat. <<WRITE_TEXT:step off canoe, boat recoils|id=ext-1>> It's the boy-on-the-board jump, just out on the lake. <<FOCUS:system-dashed-box>> And notice the beauty: this exact same idea explains a bullet sinking into a block, two carts springing apart, even a rocket firing fuel. Whenever the outside sideways push is zero, the total momentum can never change. <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:boy-momentum-arrow>> So the board didn't move by magic. It moved to keep the team's total momentum at the zero it started with. That one rule unlocks a whole shelf of problems.

9.1 CENTRE OF MASS
Suppose a spin bowler throws a cricket ball
vertically upward. Being a spinner, his fingers turn
while throwing the ball and the ball goes up spinning
rapidly. Focus your attention to a particular point on
the surface of the ball. How does it move in the space ?
Because the ball is spinning as well as rising up, in
general, the path of a particle at the surface is
complicated, not confined to a straight line or to a
plane. The centre of the ball, however, still goes on the
vertical straight line and the spinner’s fingers could
not make its path complicated. If he does not throw
the ball vertically up, rather passes it to his fellow
fielder, the centre of the ball goes in a parabola.
All the points of the ball do not go in parabolic
paths. If the ball is spinning, the paths of most of the
particles of the ball are complicated. But the centre of
the ball always goes in a parabola irrespective of how
the ball is thrown. (In fact the presence of air makes
the path of the centre slightly different from a parabola
and bowlers utilise this deviation. This effect will be
discussed in a later chapter. At present we neglect it.)
The centre of the ball is a very special point which
is called the centre of mass of the ball. Its motion is
just like the motion of a single particle thrown.

Example 9.2
   Two identical uniform rods AB and CD, each of length
L are jointed to form a T-shaped frame as shown in
figure (9.6). Locate the centre of mass of the frame. The

C of the rod AB as the origin and CD as the Y-axis. The
rod AB has mass m and its centre of mass is at C. For
the calculation of the centre of mass of the combined
system, AB may be replaced by a point particle of mass
m placed at the point C. Similarly the rod CD may be
replaced by a point particle of mass m placed at the
centre E of the rod CD. Thus, the frame is equivalent
to a system of two particles of equal masses m each,
placed at C and E. The centre of mass of this pair of
particles will be at the middle point F of CE.

CD at a distance L/4 from C.
topics.our_understanding:
Let me start with a picture you'll recognize. Imagine a spin bowler tossing a cricket ball straight up, fingers twisting so the ball spins rapidly as it rises. Now pick one tiny spot on the surface of the ball and try to follow it. Its path is a tangled mess, looping and twisting through space. But here's the magic: the very center of the ball travels in a clean, simple straight line up and down. And if the bowler throws the ball forward instead, that same center traces a smooth parabola, no matter how wildly the surface points dance around. This special point is called the centre of mass, and its motion is exactly like that of a single particle thrown into the air. That's why it matters so much: instead of tracking every messy point of a complicated object, we can track one point and describe the overall motion beautifully.

So how do we find this point? Imagine you have a collection of particles, each with its own mass and its own position. For the x-direction, you multiply each particle's mass by its x-coordinate, add all those products together, and then divide by the total mass of the whole system. That gives you the x-coordinate of the centre of mass. You do the very same thing for y and for z. In words, the centre of mass is the mass-weighted average position of all the particles. Heavier particles pull the centre of mass closer to themselves.

For the simplest case of just two particles, the centre of mass always sits on the straight line joining them. And it divides that line in the inverse ratio of the masses, meaning it lies closer to the heavier particle. If one mass is much bigger, the centre of mass sits almost right on top of it.

There's one more wonderfully practical idea here. Suppose you've already found the centre of mass of one group of particles and of another group. To find the combined centre of mass, you can pretend each group is a single point particle, with all its mass located at its own centre of mass. Then you just find the centre of mass of those two points. This lets you break a big, complicated object into simpler pieces and combine them step by step.

topics.our_understanding:
So far we've found the centre of mass by adding up lots of separate particles. But what if matter isn't in neat little chunks? What if it's spread out smoothly, like a solid rod or a curved wire? For these continuous bodies, we can't do a simple sum. Instead, we slice the body into tiny pieces, each with a tiny mass we call dm, and we add up the contributions of all those tiny pieces using integration. Integration is really just a very careful way of adding up infinitely many infinitely small things. So the centre of mass coordinates become an integral of x times dm, divided by the total mass M, and similarly for y and z.

The trick is always the same: pick a clever element, figure out the mass of that element, figure out where it sits, then integrate over the whole body. Let me walk you through the three cases the book uses. First, a uniform straight rod. Imagine you put the left end at the origin and lay the rod along the x-axis. A tiny slice between x and x plus dx has a mass that's just the mass per unit length times dx. When you do the integral, the answer comes out to be L over two — exactly the middle of the rod. That should feel right, because a uniform rod is perfectly balanced at its centre.

Next, a semicircular wire. Here we slice it by angle. Sweep a radius from zero up to pi, and each tiny sweep of angle gives a little arc of the wire. Because of symmetry, the x-coordinate of the centre of mass is zero, but the y-coordinate comes out to be two R over pi. Notice the centre of mass sits in empty space, not on the wire itself — that's perfectly allowed.

Finally, a semicircular plate. The beautiful idea here is that we build the plate out of nested semicircular wires. Each thin ring is itself a semicircular wire whose centre of mass we already know. We replace each ring by a point mass at its own centre of mass, then integrate from radius zero to R. The answer is four R over three pi. The big lesson: once you've solved a simpler shape, you can reuse it as a building block for a harder one.

The x-coordinate of the centre of mass is zero by symmetry.

topics.standalone_narration_text: <<FOCUS:rod-body>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:centre_of_mass_linear_momentum_collision:9_2:rod_slice>> You know how to balance two weights on a seesaw, but where exactly does a smooth, solid rod balance, when there are no separate weights at all? <<PAUSE:long>> Up to now we found the centre of mass by adding up separate particles, one mass here, another mass there. But this rod isn't chunks, it's matter spread out smoothly, with no gaps to point at. <<POINT:rod-body>> <<FOCUS:origin-mark>> So here is the whole idea: if we can't point at separate pieces, we'll make our own. <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:slice-element>> <<SECTION:Slicing the rod|id=sec-slice>>Watch this thin slice. We cut out one tiny piece of the rod between position x and a tiny bit further along, and we call its tiny mass dm. <<TRACE:slice-element>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:slice-element>> <<ANIMATE_PARAM:x_pos|to=0.95|from=0.05|duration=2200>> <<WRITE_TEXT:dm = a tiny piece of the rod|id=text-dm>>Now I'll slide that slice along the rod, and as it sweeps from the left end all the way to the right end, those tiny pieces cover the entire body. <<FOCUS:slice-position>> Each slice sits at its own distance x from the origin, and that distance is exactly what we measure here. <<POINT:slice-position>> Because the rod is uniform, every centimetre carries the same mass, so the mass of a slice is the mass per unit length times the slice's tiny width. <<WRITE_EQUATION:dm = \frac{M}{L}\,dx|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<FOCUS:slice-element>> So here's the honest question: if every slice has its own little mass dm at its own position x, how do we possibly combine all of them into one balance point? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:rod-body>> We add them up. Each slice contributes its position x times its mass dm, and we sum that over every slice in the body. That continuous summing-up is exactly what integration means. <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:rod-body>> <<WRITE_KEY:X = (1/M) integral of x dm|id=key-com>>Then we divide by the total mass M, and out pops the single x-coordinate of the centre of mass. <<PAUSE:short>> The x-coordinate of the centre of mass is the sum of each slice's position times its mass, divided by the total mass. <<WRITE_EQUATION:X = \frac{1}{M}\int x\,dm|id=eq-2|boxed>> <<FOCUS:slice-element>> The recipe never changes: pick a clever slice, find its mass dm, find where it sits, then integrate over the whole body. Here's an example from the chapter: finding the centre of mass of a uniform straight rod. Let M and L be the mass and the length of the rod respectively. We take the left end of the rod as the origin, with the X-axis running along the rod. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Find the centre of mass of a uniform rod of mass M and length L.|id=ex-q-1>> We start by slicing the rod into a thin element between the positions x and x plus dx. Since the rod is uniform, the mass per unit length is M divided by L, so the mass of this little element is dm equals M over L times dx. The coordinates of the element are x, zero, zero. <<WRITE_STEP:dm = (M/L) dx, element at (x, 0, 0)|id=ex-step-1-1>> Now the x-coordinate of the centre of mass is one over M times the integral of x dm. Substituting dm equals M over L times dx, and letting x vary from zero to L, this becomes one over M times the integral from zero to L of x times M over L dx. <<WRITE_STEP:X = (1/M) ∫ x dm = (1/M) ∫₀ᴸ x (M/L) dx|id=ex-step-1-2>> The M's cancel, leaving one over L times x squared over two, evaluated from zero to L. Plugging in the limits gives one over L times L squared over two, which simplifies to L over two. <<WRITE_STEP:X = (1/L)[x²/2]₀ᴸ = L/2|id=ex-step-1-3>> By symmetry the y-coordinate is zero and the z-coordinate is zero as well. So the answer is that the centre of mass sits at L over two, zero, zero, exactly the middle point of the rod. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Centre of mass at (L/2, 0, 0) — the middle of the rod|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter. We have a uniform semicircular wire of mass M and radius R. We take its centre as the origin, with the line joining the ends along the X-axis, and the Y-axis in the plane of the wire. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Find the centre of mass of a uniform semicircular wire, mass M, radius R.|id=ex-q-1>> We start by picking an element. Take a radius making an angle theta with the X-axis, and rotate it further by a small angle d theta. This gives an element of length R times d theta. As theta is increased from zero to pi, the whole wire is covered. <<WRITE_STEP:element length = R d theta, theta from 0 to pi|id=ex-step-1-1>> The coordinates of this element are R cos theta and R sin theta. Since the wire is uniform, the mass per unit length is M divided by pi R. So the mass of the element, d m, equals M over pi R times R d theta, which simplifies to M over pi times d theta. <<WRITE_STEP:element at (R cos theta, R sin theta)|id=ex-step-1-2>><<WRITE_EQUATION:dm = \frac{M}{\pi R}\,(R\,d\theta) = \frac{M}{\pi}\,d\theta|id=ex-eq-1>> Now we integrate. X is one over M times the integral from zero to pi of R cos theta times M over pi d theta. The integral of cosine over zero to pi vanishes, so X comes out zero. <<WRITE_STEP:X = (1/M) ∫₀^π (R cos theta)(M/pi) d theta = 0|id=ex-step-1-3>> Similarly, Y is one over M times the integral from zero to pi of R sin theta times M over pi d theta. The integral of sine over zero to pi gives two, so Y comes out two R over pi. <<WRITE_STEP:Y = (1/M) ∫₀^π (R sin theta)(M/pi) d theta = 2R/pi|id=ex-step-1-4>> And the answer is: the centre of mass is at zero, two R over pi. Notice it sits on the Y-axis, in empty space off the wire itself. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Centre of mass at (0, 2R/pi)|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter: finding the centre of mass of a uniform semicircular plate. Let the mass of the plate be M and the radius be R. We put the origin at the centre, with the X-axis along the straight edge and the Y-axis in the plane of the plate. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Find centre of mass of a uniform semicircular plate, mass M, radius R|id=ex-q-1>> The trick is to build the plate from nested semicircular wires. Draw a semicircle of radius r and another of radius r plus dr; the element is the ring between radius r and r plus dr. The area of this ring element is pi times r times dr. <<WRITE_STEP:Element = semicircular ring between r and r + dr|id=ex-step-1>><<WRITE_EQUATION:dA = \pi r\,dr|id=ex-eq-1>> Now the whole area of the plate is pi R squared over two, so the mass per unit area is M divided by pi R squared over two. Multiplying that by the element's area gives the mass of the element as two M r dr over R squared. <<WRITE_STEP:Area of plate = pi R squared over 2, so mass per area = M / (pi R squared / 2)|id=ex-step-2>><<WRITE_EQUATION:dm = \dfrac{2 M r\,dr}{R^{2}}|id=ex-eq-2>> Each wire element is itself a semicircle, and the centre of mass of each wire is at two r over pi. So we integrate this y-coordinate weighted by the element mass, letting r go from zero to R. <<WRITE_STEP:y of each wire = 2r/pi; integrate r from 0 to R|id=ex-step-3>><<WRITE_EQUATION:Y = \dfrac{1}{M}\int_{0}^{R}\dfrac{2r}{\pi}\cdot\dfrac{2Mr}{R^{2}}\,dr|id=ex-eq-3>> Working the integral out gives one over M times four M over pi R squared times R cubed over three, and that simplifies to four R over three pi. By symmetry, the x-coordinate is zero. So the centre of mass sits at Y equals four R over three pi. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Y = 4R / (3 pi),  X = 0 by symmetry|id=ex-ans-1>> You've balanced this yourself. Lay a wooden spoon flat across one finger and slide it until it stops tipping. There's exactly one spot where it rests, and for a nice uniform stick that spot sits right at the middle, at L over two. That balance point you found by feel is precisely the centre of mass we just got from slicing the rod into tiny pieces and integrating x times dm. Here's something wild about this. For that semicircular wire, the centre of mass lands at two R over pi, which sits in empty space, completely off the wire itself. <<WRITE_KEY:centre of mass can sit in empty space|id=ext-key-1>> The same thing happens with a boomerang or a curved banana, they spin about a point that isn't even part of the object. That's the whole point of the calculation: the centre of mass is just a weighted average of position, and nothing says that average has to land on the material. <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:com-point>> For a uniform rod the slices are perfectly balanced left and right, so the centre of mass lands exactly in the middle, right here. <<FOCUS:com-point>> So a smooth body has no separate weights to add, but by slicing it into infinitely many tiny dm pieces and integrating, we found its balance point anyway.

topics.our_understanding:
Let's think about how the centre of mass of a system moves. Imagine two particles, A and B, sitting on a line. They attract each other and start to move toward one another. They push and pull on each other, but those are internal forces — forces between members of the same system. Here's the beautiful result: even as the particles speed up and rush together, their centre of mass doesn't move at all, as long as no outside force acts on them.

Why does this happen? The velocity of the centre of mass is just a weighted average of the velocities of the particles, weighted by their masses. The acceleration of the centre of mass is the weighted average of their accelerations. Now, particle A feels a force F toward B, and particle B feels exactly the opposite force, F toward A. When you put these into the formula for the acceleration of the centre of mass, the mass cancels with the force in each term — one gives plus F and the other gives minus F — and they add up to zero. So the centre of mass has zero acceleration. If it started at rest, it stays at rest.

This isn't just for two particles. For any number of particles, the internal forces always cancel in pairs because of Newton's third law — every push has an equal and opposite push back. So when you add up all the forces in the system, only the external forces survive. The grand result is this: the total mass times the acceleration of the centre of mass equals the total external force. 

Think about what that means. The centre of mass behaves exactly like a single imaginary particle, carrying the whole mass of the system, pushed only by the external forces. If the external forces add to zero, the centre of mass either stays put or keeps gliding in a straight line at constant speed, no matter how complicated the individual paths are. And here's a striking picture: throw a spinning ball, and its centre traces a parabola. If the ball suddenly breaks into two pieces in mid-air, each piece flies off on its own curve — but their centre of mass keeps gliding along that same original parabola, as if nothing had happened. The internal explosion changes nothing about the centre of mass.

The attraction between the particles is purely internal to the system. So the sum of external forces on the system is zero, which means the centre of mass has no acceleration. <<WRITE_STEP:External force on system = 0, so a of centre of mass = 0|id=ex-step-1-1>> Now both particles start at rest, so the velocity of the centre of mass is zero. With zero acceleration and zero initial velocity, the centre of mass simply never moves. <<WRITE_STEP:Both start at rest, so velocity of centre of mass = 0, centre of mass stays fixed|id=ex-step-1-2>> At the moment of collision, both particles are at one single place, and the centre of mass must also be at that very place. But since the centre of mass hasn't moved at all, the collision happens exactly at the centre of mass. <<WRITE_STEP:At collision both particles coincide with centre of mass, so collision occurs at the centre of mass|id=ex-step-1-3>> Finally we locate that point. The centre of mass sits at a distance two d over three from the initial position of the particle of mass m, toward the other particle. <<WRITE_EQUATION:x_{cm} = \frac{2d}{3}|id=ex-eq-1>> And so the answer is: the collision takes place at the centre of mass, a distance two d over three from the initial position of the particle of mass m, toward the other particle. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Collision occurs at the centre of mass, 2d/3 from the mass m, toward the mass 2m|id=ex-ans-1>> Watch a diver next time the Olympics are on. They leap off the board, fold into a tuck, spin through a couple of somersaults, and slice into the water. Their arms and legs are flying around in wild arcs — but there's one point in their body that doesn't care about any of that. <<WRITE_TEXT:diver's centre of mass = clean parabola|id=ext-1>> The centre of mass traces a single smooth parabola from the board straight down to the water. And that's exactly what we just proved. Once they're airborne, gravity is the only external force acting. All the twisting of the limbs is internal — it can't move the centre of mass off its parabola. The somersaults rearrange the body around that point, but the point itself glides on, as if a single particle had been tossed into the air. Here's something wild to think about the next time you watch fireworks. The shell arcs up into the sky, and then — bang — it bursts into hundreds of sparks flying outward in every direction. But the explosion is entirely an internal force. So even though the sparks scatter everywhere, the centre of mass of that whole glowing cloud keeps gliding along the very same parabola the shell was already following, as if the explosion never happened. The fireworks designers are quietly relying on Newton's third law every single show. If it can't accelerate, its velocity never changes. And since these two started at rest, the centre of mass stays nailed in place — internal forces alone can never shift it. <<POINT:com-point>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:com-point>> That's the deep idea: no matter how violently the parts of a system push and pull each other, only an outside force can move their centre of mass.

topics.our_understanding:
Let's talk about linear momentum, which is one of the most useful ideas in all of physics. The momentum of a single particle is simply its mass times its velocity. Since velocity has a direction, momentum is also a vector — it points the same way the particle is moving. Now, if you have a whole system made of many particles, the total momentum is just the vector sum of each particle's individual momentum. Here's the beautiful part: when you add all those up, it turns out the total momentum equals the total mass of the system times the velocity of the centre of mass. So instead of tracking every single particle, you can describe the momentum of the whole system with just one number for mass and one velocity — the velocity of the centre of mass.

Now comes the powerful conclusion. We learned earlier that if the external forces on a system add up to zero, the centre of mass moves with constant velocity. And since total momentum equals total mass times that centre of mass velocity, this means the total momentum stays constant too — constant in both size and direction. This is the principle of conservation of linear momentum. It's a big deal because it lets you predict what happens after an event without knowing the messy details of the internal forces.

Think about a simple case first: a single particle with no force on it. Watched from an inertial frame, it just drifts along at steady velocity, so its momentum never changes. That's conservation in its simplest form.

Now picture something more interesting — a radioactive nucleus sitting at rest that suddenly spits out an alpha particle. Take the whole nucleus as your system. The alpha particle gets flung out because of nuclear forces between the protons and neutrons. But notice — those are internal forces, not external ones. There's no external push, so the total momentum can't change. Before the emission everything was at rest, so the total momentum was zero. Afterward, the alpha particle flies off one way, so the leftover nucleus must recoil the opposite way. The momenta of the two pieces must cancel to keep the total at zero. The heavier residual nucleus moves slowly backward, while the lighter alpha particle zips forward fast. This is exactly why a gun kicks back when fired, and it all comes from momentum staying conserved.

After the emission, the system is broken up into two parts, the alpha particle and the residual nucleus. topics.our_understanding:
Let's talk about how a rocket actually moves, because it's one of the most beautiful uses of momentum in all of physics. Inside a rocket, fuel burns and creates hot gases. Those gases shoot out the back through a nozzle. Now here's the key idea: when the rocket pushes that gas backward, the gas pushes the rocket forward. That forward push is what makes the rocket speed up. It's momentum conservation in action — push something one way, and you get shoved the other way.

Let's set up the picture. At the start, at time zero, the rocket together with all its fuel has some total mass we'll call M naught. The gas streams out at a steady rate, meaning a fixed amount of mass leaves every second — call that rate r. And the gas leaves at a constant speed u relative to the rocket itself. Now, as time passes, the rocket keeps losing mass because it's burning fuel. So at any later time t, the mass left is M naught minus r times t. Notice the rocket is getting lighter and lighter.

To find how the rocket speeds up, we look at a tiny slice of time. In that little interval, a small chunk of gas gets ejected. Since no outside force acts on the rocket-plus-fuel system, the total momentum stays the same. When you carefully balance the momentum before and after, and let the time interval shrink toward zero, you get a wonderfully clean result. The acceleration of the rocket equals r times u, divided by the mass remaining at that moment, which is M naught minus r times t.

Now look closely at what this tells us. The top of that fraction, r times u, stays constant. But the bottom keeps shrinking because the rocket keeps losing mass. So the acceleration actually grows as time goes on. The rocket pushes harder and harder on itself, in effect, as it gets lighter. That's why rockets seem to leap faster and faster as they climb.

Finally, if we ignore gravity and add up all that acceleration over time, we get the rocket's speed. The velocity equals u times the natural logarithm of M naught divided by the mass remaining, which is M naught minus r times t. This is the famous rocket equation, and it shows that to go faster, you want fast exhaust and you want to burn away a large fraction of your starting mass.

So how does it possibly speed up? <<PAUSE:long>> <<FOCUS:gas-jet>> Here's the secret. The rocket carries its own ammunition: fuel that burns into hot gas, and that gas gets blasted out the back at high speed. <<TRACE:gas-jet>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:rocket-velocity-arrow>> <<WRITE_KEY:Throw gas backward, get shoved forward|id=key-1>>And this is the whole trick: when the rocket throws that gas backward, the gas pushes the rocket forward. That gas carries momentum backward. <<POINT:gas-momentum-arrow>> <<FOCUS:rocket-velocity-arrow>> So if the gas gained backward momentum, and the total has to stay the same, the rocket must gain exactly that much forward momentum to balance the books. <<FOCUS:rocket-body>> Let's name our quantities. It's hurling gas backward and riding the recoil — pure momentum conservation, working in empty space. <<TRACE:rocket-velocity-arrow>> <<PAUSE:short>>

9.6 COLLISION
Consider the situation shown in figure (9.13). Two
blocks of masses m1 and m2 are moving on the same
straight line on a frictionless horizontal table. The
block m2 , which is ahead of m1 , is going with a speed
v2 smaller than the speed v1 of m1 . A spring is attached
to the rear end of m2 . Since v1 > v2 , the block m1 will
touch the rear of the spring at some instant, say t1 .
Then onwards, the velocity of the left end of the spring
will be equal to the velocity of m1 (as they are in
contact). The velocity of the right end of the spring
will be same as that of m2 (as they are in contact).
Since m1 moves faster than m2 , the length of the
spring will decrease. The spring will be compressed.
As it is compressed, it pushes back both the blocks
with forces kx where x is the compression and k, the
spring constant. This force is in the direction of the
velocity of m2 , hence m2 will accelerate. However, this
is opposite to the velocity of m1 and so m1 will
decelerate. The velocity of the front block A (which was
slower initially) will gradually increase, and the
velocity of the rear block B (which was faster initially)
will gradually decrease. The spring will continue to
become more and more compressed as long as the rear
block B is faster than the front block A. There will be
an instant t1  t1 , when the two blocks will have equal
velocities. At this instant, both the ends of the spring
will move with the same velocity and no further
compression will take place. This corresponds to the
maximum compression of the spring. Thus, “the
spring-compression is maximum when the two blocks
attain equal velocities”.
Now, the spring being already compressed, it
continues to push back the two blocks. Thus, the front
block A will still be accelerated and the rear block B
will still be decelerated. At t1  t1 the velocities were
equal and hence, after t1  t1 the front block will move
faster than the rear block. And so do the ends of the
spring as they are in contact with the blocks. The
spring will thus increase its length. This process will
continue till the spring acquires its natural length, say
at a time t1  t1  t2 . Once the spring regains its
natural length, it stops exerting any force on the

Almost similar is the situation when two balls

The deformed balls push each other and the

topics.our_understanding:
Let me paint you a picture. Two blocks slide along a smooth, frictionless table in the same straight line. The block in front is moving slower, and the block behind is moving faster. On the rear of the front block there's a spring sticking out. Since the back block is catching up, at some moment it touches that spring. Now think about what happens. The left end of the spring moves with the fast back block, and the right end moves with the slow front block. Because the back is faster, the spring gets squeezed, and a squeezed spring pushes back on both blocks. It pushes the front block forward, speeding it up, and it pushes the back block backward, slowing it down. So the fast one slows and the slow one speeds up. They keep approaching the same speed. The spring keeps compressing as long as the rear block is still faster. The key insight is this: the spring reaches its maximum compression exactly when both blocks have the same velocity. At that instant there's no more squeezing happening.

After that, the spring is still compressed, so it keeps pushing. Now the front block becomes faster than the back block, the spring stretches back toward its natural length, and once it reaches that natural length it stops pushing. The blocks then separate and glide off at constant speeds.

Throughout this whole event, two big ideas hold. First, momentum. Because no outside force acts on the two-block system, the total momentum stays exactly the same before, during, and after. The spring is massless, so it pushes equally and oppositely on both blocks. Second, energy. With no friction, the kinetic energy plus the spring's stored elastic energy stays constant. When the spring is squeezed, some kinetic energy is hiding inside it as elastic potential energy. When the spring springs back, that energy returns as motion. So the kinetic energy before equals the kinetic energy after, even though it dips down in the middle.

Now replace the spring with two balls touching directly. Same story: they deform instead of compressing a spring, deformation is maximum when their speeds match, and momentum is always conserved. What happens next depends on the material. If the balls are perfectly elastic, they bounce back to their shape and give all the energy back, so final kinetic energy equals initial. If they're perfectly inelastic, they stay deformed and move together with one common velocity, losing the most kinetic energy. Partially elastic balls fall in between, losing some but not all of that energy.

topics.our_understanding:
Let's picture two objects moving along the same straight line. Call them A and B. Object A has some mass and moves to the right with a certain velocity, and object B is ahead of it moving in the same direction but slower. Because A is faster, it eventually catches up and collides with B. After they hit, both have new velocities, and our job is to figure out what those new velocities are.

We have two powerful tools. The first is conservation of linear momentum, which says the total momentum before the collision equals the total momentum after. The second tool only applies when the collision is elastic, meaning no kinetic energy is lost. So the total kinetic energy before equals the total kinetic energy after.

Here's the beautiful part. When you take the kinetic energy equation and the momentum equation and divide one by the other, all the squared terms simplify and you get a wonderfully simple result. It says the velocity of separation after the collision equals the velocity of approach before the collision. In plain words, the rate at which the two bodies were closing in on each other before the hit equals the rate at which they fly apart after the hit. That single idea makes elastic collision problems much easier to solve.

Using momentum conservation together with this separation rule, we can solve for both final velocities in terms of the masses and the starting velocities. Those two formulas are the workhorses of this topic.

Now let's look at some special cases that build your intuition. First, imagine a very heavy body hitting a much lighter body from behind. The heavy one barely notices and keeps moving at almost the same speed, while the light one gets kicked forward. If the light body started at rest, it flies off at double the heavy body's velocity. Next, flip it around: a light body hits a heavy body from behind. The heavy one keeps moving as if nothing happened, but the light one bounces back. If the heavy body was at rest, the light one returns with almost the same speed it came in with. That's exactly what happens when a ball bounces off a fixed wall.

Finally, the most elegant case: two bodies of equal mass. When they collide elastically, they simply swap velocities. The first takes on the second's speed, and the second takes on the first's. Watch this on a billiards table sometime and you'll see it happen right before your eyes.

topics.our_understanding:
Let's talk about a special kind of collision called a perfectly inelastic collision. The key idea here is simple to picture: imagine two objects that crash into each other and then stick together, moving along afterward as one single combined lump. Think of two lumps of clay slamming together, or two railway carts that latch on when they meet. After the collision, they share one common velocity because they're now effectively one body.

So how do we find that common velocity? We lean on the great rule that always holds in collisions, the conservation of linear momentum. The total momentum before the crash must equal the total momentum after. Before the collision, each object carries its own momentum, which is its mass times its velocity. After the collision, the combined mass, which is the sum of the two masses, moves at one shared velocity. Setting those equal and solving, the common velocity equals the total momentum before, divided by the total mass. In words, take the first mass times its velocity, add the second mass times its velocity, and divide that whole thing by the sum of the two masses. That gives you the speed they move off with together.

Now here's something really important. Momentum is conserved, yes, but kinetic energy is not. When objects stick together, some of the energy that was in motion gets lost. Where does it go? It turns into heat, sound, and into deforming or squashing the objects. The textbook works out exactly how much kinetic energy is lost, and after some algebra the loss comes out to the first mass times the second mass, times the square of the difference of their velocities, all divided by twice the sum of the masses.

Notice that this loss is always positive. That means kinetic energy always decreases in a perfectly inelastic collision. It can never increase. And notice it depends on how different the two velocities are. If both objects were moving at the same speed in the same direction, the difference would be zero and no energy would be lost, which makes sense because then there's really no collision happening at all. The bigger the difference in their velocities, the more energy gets converted away. This is the most extreme case of energy loss in any collision, because the objects lose all their relative motion when they stick together.

They merge into one blob and keep moving. So where did all that bouncing energy go? <<PAUSE:long>> <<FOCUS:mass-b>> This is what physicists call a perfectly inelastic collision: the two objects crash and then stick together, travelling on as a single combined lump. <<SECTION:Perfectly Inelastic Collision|id=sec-1>><<WRITE_TEXT:Objects stick, move as one|id=text-1>> <<POINT:mass-b>> <<FOCUS:velocity-a>> Here are our two objects before the crash. Mass m one slides in from the left with velocity v one, and mass m two comes the other way with velocity v two. <<POINT:velocity-a>> <<ANIMATE_PARAM:t|to=1.0|from=0.0|duration=2200>> Watch what happens as they meet — they don't rebound, they fuse, and the new combined object moves off with one single shared velocity, capital V. <<TRACE:combined-lump>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:combined-velocity>> Now, how on earth do we find that one shared velocity? We reach for the rule that never lets us down in a collision: the total momentum afterwards must equal the total momentum before. <<PAUSE:short>> Before the crash, each object carries its own momentum, mass times velocity, so the total is m one times v one plus m two times v two. <<POINT:velocity-b>> <<FOCUS:combined-lump>> After the crash there's just one lump, with the combined mass m one plus m two, all moving at that single velocity capital V. <<WRITE_STEP:Before equals after: m1 v1 plus m2 v2 equals (m1 plus m2) V|id=step-1>> The total momentum before, mass times velocity for each object, equals the combined mass times the single shared velocity after. <<WRITE_EQUATION:m_1 v_1 + m_2 v_2 = (m_1 + m_2)V|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<FOCUS:combined-velocity>> Setting before equal to after and rearranging, the shared velocity is simply the total momentum divided by the total mass. That's the whole secret of a sticky collision. <<WRITE_KEY:V equals total momentum over total mass|id=key-1>> <<PAUSE:short>> The shared velocity is just the total momentum divided by the total mass. <<WRITE_EQUATION:V = \dfrac{m_1 v_1 + m_2 v_2}{m_1 + m_2}|id=eq-2|boxed>> <<FOCUS:combined-lump>> But here's the puzzle. Momentum was perfectly conserved — so was the kinetic energy conserved too? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:combined-velocity>> No. If you add up one half m v squared before and after, the after is always smaller. Energy went missing — it became heat, sound, and the work of squashing the clay. <<WRITE_TEXT:KE lost to heat, sound, deformation|id=text-2>> <<PAUSE:short>> The kinetic energy lost depends on the masses and on the square of how fast they were closing in on each other, and it's always positive. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\Delta KE = \dfrac{m_1 m_2 (v_1 - v_2)^2}{2(m_1 + m_2)}|id=eq-3|boxed>> <<FOCUS:combined-lump>> So remember the two halves of this story: momentum is always conserved, which gives us the shared velocity, but kinetic energy is not — some of it is lost in the sticking. <<WRITE_KEY:Momentum conserved, KE lost|id=key-2>> <<PAUSE:short>>
